flashcards.front: Password hash sync vs. pass-through authentication vs. federation
flashcards.back: Password hash sync replicates a hash of the on-premises password hash to Entra ID, so sign-in works even if on-premises infrastructure is briefly unavailable. Pass-through authentication validates each sign-in directly against on-premises AD in real time via a lightweight agent, with no password data stored in the cloud. Federation (AD FS) delegates authentication entirely to an on-premises identity provider.
flashcards.detail: Pass-through authentication needs at least one authentication agent online to work at all, which is a resilience trade-off compared to password hash sync.

flashcards.back: Conditional Access is a policy engine that evaluates signals (user, device, location, risk) at sign-in time and applies controls in response. MFA is one of the controls Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy system of its own.
flashcards.detail: A Conditional Access policy could require MFA only for risky sign-ins or unmanaged devices, rather than requiring it for every sign-in unconditionally.

flashcards.back: Grants just-in-time, time-bound elevation to privileged roles, optionally requiring approval and justification, instead of leaving administrators with standing (always-on) privileged access.
flashcards.detail: PIM and Conditional Access solve different problems and are commonly layered together, such as requiring MFA (a Conditional Access control) as a condition of activating a PIM-eligible role.

flashcards.back: Access reviews periodically recertify access that already exists, so an administrator (or the resource owner) confirms it should continue or revokes it. Entitlement management bundles resources into requestable access packages with approval workflows and built-in, automatic expiration for new access.
flashcards.detail: A scenario about access to time-boxed contractor or project work usually points to entitlement management; a scenario about periodically re-certifying existing standing access points to access reviews.

flashcards.front: Management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups
flashcards.back: Management groups group subscriptions so policy and RBAC can be assigned once and inherited down across an organization. Subscriptions are billing and scale boundaries. Resource groups are deployment and lifecycle containers within a subscription.
flashcards.detail: Management groups don't replace resource groups — they sit above subscriptions in the hierarchy, while resource groups remain the deployment boundary inside each subscription.

flashcards.front: Azure Policy effects: Deny, Audit, and DeployIfNotExists
flashcards.back: Deny blocks the creation or update of a noncompliant resource outright. Audit flags noncompliant resources for visibility without blocking anything. DeployIfNotExists automatically remediates by deploying a related resource (like a diagnostic setting) when a required one is missing.
flashcards.detail: Only DeployIfNotExists actively fixes existing noncompliant resources; Audit only reports on them, and Deny only stops new noncompliant ones from being created.

flashcards.back: A landing zone is a pre-provisioned environment — management group hierarchy, policy, identity, and hub networking — built on the Cloud Adoption Framework, so every new subscription starts from a consistent, governed baseline instead of each team configuring governance independently.
flashcards.detail: Landing zones are the recommended starting point for any new enterprise Azure environment on the exam, not just a nice-to-have.

flashcards.front: Log Analytics workspace design: centralized vs. decentralized
flashcards.back: A centralized workspace simplifies cross-resource queries and gives a single place to see cost and usage, but has coarser access boundaries. Decentralized (per-team or per-subscription) workspaces give finer access control, retention, and data-sovereignty boundaries, at the cost of harder cross-workspace querying.
flashcards.detail: A regulated subsidiary that needs its own retention and access boundary is a strong signal for a dedicated workspace, even inside an otherwise centralized design.

flashcards.back: Metrics are lightweight numerical time-series data, well suited to fast, near-real-time alerting on things like CPU or memory thresholds. Logs are structured or free-form records stored in a Log Analytics workspace, queried with KQL, and suited to deep, multi-table investigation.
flashcards.detail: Reaching for Logs for a simple, fast threshold alert adds unnecessary query latency; reaching for Metrics for a complex correlation query doesn't have the structure to support it.

flashcards.front: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on a VM
flashcards.back: Azure SQL Database (single database) is fully managed PaaS with the least administrative overhead but limited instance-level features. SQL Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility (SQL Agent, cross-database queries, linked servers) while staying PaaS. SQL Server on a VM gives full OS and engine control (IaaS) for maximum compatibility, at the cost of managing patching yourself.
flashcards.detail: A migration that depends on SQL Agent jobs or cross-database queries but still wants to avoid managing the OS points squarely at Managed Instance, not SQL Database.

flashcards.back: Five levels, from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, and Eventual. Strong gives no staleness but the highest latency and lowest availability; Eventual gives the lowest latency and highest availability but no ordering guarantee.
flashcards.detail: Session is the default and fits most single-user scenarios that need to see their own writes immediately; Eventual fits read-heavy workloads (like a shared catalog) that can tolerate a few seconds of staleness in exchange for speed.

flashcards.back: A good partition key has high cardinality and spreads requests and storage evenly. A low-cardinality key concentrates traffic on a small number of physical partitions, creating a "hot partition" that throttles throughput no matter how much RU/s is provisioned.
flashcards.detail: The fix for a hot partition is redesigning the partition key itself, not raising the consistency level or adding more provisioned throughput.

flashcards.front: Storage redundancy: LRS, ZRS, GRS, and GZRS
flashcards.back: LRS keeps three synchronous copies within one datacenter. ZRS spreads synchronous copies across availability zones in the same region. GRS asynchronously replicates to a paired secondary region (without zone redundancy locally). GZRS combines zone redundancy in the primary region with geo-replication to a secondary region.
flashcards.detail: Only the "RA-" (read-access) variants of GRS/GZRS let an application read from the secondary region before an actual failover occurs.

flashcards.front: Access tiers: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive
flashcards.back: Hot suits frequently accessed data at the highest storage cost and lowest access cost. Cool and Cold suit infrequently accessed data, with lower storage cost but higher access cost and longer minimum retention. Archive is the cheapest tier for rarely accessed data, but blobs must be rehydrated (a process that can take hours) before they can be read.
flashcards.detail: A cost-first requirement with an acceptable multi-hour retrieval delay is the signal for Archive; needing the data readable at any moment rules Archive out even if it's rarely accessed.

flashcards.back: Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace enabled, purpose-built for large-scale analytics (Synapse, Databricks, HDInsight) that need POSIX-like access control lists and efficient directory-level operations, not just flat object storage.
flashcards.detail: The hierarchical namespace is what turns general-purpose Blob storage into a proper data lake for big-data analytics engines.

flashcards.front: Data Migration Assistant (DMA) vs. Database Migration Service (DMS)
flashcards.back: DMA assesses an on-premises database for compatibility issues and deprecated features before any migration happens. DMS performs the actual migration — online (minimal downtime) or offline — into the target Azure data service.
flashcards.detail: DMA answers "will this break after we move it?"; DMS is the tool that actually moves the data once you're ready to go.

flashcards.back: A private endpoint gives a PaaS resource a private IP address inside your VNet, reachable privately even from on-premises or peered networks, and can remove its public endpoint entirely. A service endpoint keeps the resource's public IP but optimizes and restricts routing for traffic that already originates from a specific subnet.
flashcards.detail: Only a private endpoint lets on-premises traffic, arriving over ExpressRoute or a VPN, reach a PaaS service privately — a service endpoint only helps traffic that already starts inside the VNet.

flashcards.front: Azure Backup vs. Azure Site Recovery
flashcards.back: Azure Backup protects data, restoring files, VMs, or databases to a prior point in time. Azure Site Recovery protects availability, replicating an entire VM or workload to a secondary region or zone so it can fail over and keep running through an outage.
flashcards.detail: A request to recover an accidentally deleted file points to Backup; a request to keep an application running after a regional outage points to Site Recovery.

flashcards.back: Availability zones give synchronous, low-latency redundancy across physically separate datacenters within one region, protecting against a single-datacenter loss. A secondary region provides asynchronous DR redundancy against a full regional disaster, at the cost of higher replication latency.
flashcards.detail: Zones and a secondary region solve two different failure scopes, and a well-designed solution frequently uses both together rather than choosing one over the other.

flashcards.back: Group one or more databases on a logical server, replicate them to a secondary region, and expose stable read-write and read-only listener endpoints that automatically redirect after a failover, so application connection strings never need to change.
flashcards.detail: The read-only listener can serve reads from the secondary region even before any failover occurs, not only afterward.

flashcards.front: RTO and RPO drive the architecture, not the other way around
flashcards.back: Business requirements set the maximum tolerable downtime (RTO) and data loss (RPO) first. The backup frequency, replication approach, and failover automation are then designed to meet those numbers, rather than being chosen first and having the numbers backfilled to match.
flashcards.detail: A design question that states specific RTO/RPO numbers is really asking you to pick the cheapest architecture that still satisfies both, not the most impressive-sounding one.

flashcards.back: The container that stores Azure Backup data and Azure Site Recovery replication configuration and metadata. A single vault can hold both backup and Site Recovery items, and the vault's own redundancy setting — LRS, GRS, or Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) — determines whether it survives a regional loss.
flashcards.detail: It's easy to assume backups automatically survive a regional outage — that depends entirely on the vault's own storage redundancy setting, which is worth checking explicitly.

flashcards.back: Active-active runs full production traffic in two or more regions simultaneously, giving the fastest possible RTO at the highest cost and complexity (including handling multi-region write conflicts). Active-passive keeps a warm or cold standby region that only takes traffic after a failover, which is cheaper but slower to recover.
flashcards.detail: "Zero perceptible downtime during a regional failure" is the signal phrase for active-active; any standby that needs to be activated first, warm or cold, is active-passive.

flashcards.front: Choosing compute: VM vs. App Service vs. AKS vs. Container Apps vs. Functions
flashcards.back: VMs give full OS control for legacy or specialized workloads. App Service is managed PaaS web hosting with no orchestration to manage. AKS gives full Kubernetes control for complex microservices needing custom orchestration. Container Apps runs serverless containers with built-in autoscaling and microservices features, without managing a cluster. Functions is event-driven, per-execution billed compute for short-lived triggered code.
flashcards.detail: "Wants container-based autoscaling but doesn't want to manage a cluster" is the classic signal for Container Apps over AKS.

flashcards.back: A central hub VNet hosts shared services — firewall, VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, DNS — while spoke VNets (one per workload or team) peer only to the hub, not to each other, centralizing connectivity, inspection, and cost.
flashcards.detail: By default, peering to a shared hub does not let two spokes talk to each other directly — that isolation is often the whole point of the design. An Azure landing zone typically ships this topology already built for new workloads to land into.

flashcards.front: VNet peering vs. VPN Gateway vs. ExpressRoute
flashcards.back: VNet peering connects Azure VNets directly over Microsoft's backbone, with low latency and no gateway required. A Site-to-Site VPN Gateway connects on-premises networks to Azure over an encrypted tunnel across the public internet. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit to Azure through a connectivity provider, bypassing the public internet for higher, more predictable bandwidth.
flashcards.detail: ExpressRoute is the answer whenever a scenario needs the most predictable bandwidth and latency and is willing to work with a connectivity provider for a dedicated circuit.

flashcards.front: Azure Front Door vs. Application Gateway vs. Traffic Manager
flashcards.back: Front Door is a global, layer-7 entry point with edge caching, a Web Application Firewall, and routing across regions. Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer that can also provide a Web Application Firewall, but only within one region. Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing with no data-plane inspection — it only returns which endpoint's IP address to use.
flashcards.detail: Because Traffic Manager works purely at the DNS layer, its failover is limited by client-side DNS caching (TTL), unlike Front Door's real data-plane failover.

flashcards.front: Network security group (NSG) vs. Azure Firewall
flashcards.back: An NSG is a per-subnet or per-NIC allow/deny filter on IP address, port, and protocol — simple and free. Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, centralized firewall supporting FQDN-based filtering and unified logging across many VNets, suited to enforcing a perimeter from a hub.
flashcards.detail: NSGs have no concept of a fully qualified domain name — FQDN-based outbound filtering across a whole hub-and-spoke estate calls for Azure Firewall, not a pile of per-subnet NSGs.

flashcards.back: The hub service for discovering on-premises servers and workloads, assessing them (right-sizing, readiness, cost estimation), and coordinating the actual migration tools, all before any workload is moved.
flashcards.detail: Azure Migrate is the answer for the discovery-and-assessment phase; the actual data move is often handed off to a more specialized tool like the Database Migration Service.

flashcards.front: Service Bus vs. Event Grid vs. Event Hubs
flashcards.back: Service Bus is a message broker for ordered, transactional, point-to-point or pub/sub messaging with guaranteed delivery. Event Grid is a lightweight, reactive eventing service for discrete event notifications with push-based routing. Event Hubs is built for high-throughput streaming and telemetry ingestion at massive scale.
flashcards.detail: A requirement for reliable, ordered, exactly-processed order queues points to Service Bus; a requirement to react to "a blob was created" points to Event Grid; high-volume telemetry ingestion points to Event Hubs.

flashcards.back: A facade placed in front of backend APIs, regardless of where or how they're hosted, adding a consistent gateway for authentication, rate limiting, versioning, and a developer portal, decoupling API consumers from the underlying implementation.
flashcards.detail: API Management is the answer whenever multiple differently-hosted backends need one consistent, versioned, authenticated surface for external or partner consumers.

flashcards.front: Logic Apps vs. Azure Functions for integration
flashcards.back: Logic Apps is a low-code, designer-driven workflow orchestrator with hundreds of prebuilt connectors, suited to integrating SaaS and enterprise systems. Azure Functions is code-first, event-triggered compute, better suited when custom logic or fine-grained execution control is the priority.
flashcards.detail: A requirement that business analysts, not just developers, be able to understand and adjust the flow is a strong signal for Logic Apps over hand-written Functions code.

flashcards.back: A Microsoft-managed networking service that automates large-scale hub-and-spoke connectivity — branch, VPN, and ExpressRoute connections, hubs, and routing — across many regions, instead of building and peering each hub manually.
flashcards.detail: Virtual WAN is the answer when a design needs to scale hub-and-spoke connectivity across many regions without hand-configuring peering and routing for every hub.

flashcards.front: Scale up vs. scale out for App Service
flashcards.back: Scaling up changes the App Service plan's pricing tier or size to a bigger instance. Scaling out adds more instances of the same tier, often automated through autoscale rules based on metrics or a schedule.
flashcards.detail: Autoscale rules configure scaling out (more instances); changing to a larger tier is always a manual or scripted scale-up decision, not something autoscale rules do on their own.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's end-to-end guidance for an organization's cloud journey — strategy, planning, readiness, adoption, governance, and management — that Azure landing zones are the concrete, deployable implementation of.
flashcards.detail: CAF is the "why and how to think about it" methodology; a landing zone is the actual environment you get by following it.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's set of five pillars — reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency — used to evaluate architectural trade-offs against each other rather than optimizing any one in isolation.
flashcards.detail: AZ-305 exam scenarios are frequently a trade-off between two of these pillars — recognizing which one the scenario is actually prioritizing is often the real question being asked.

flashcards.back: Synchronously replicates data across three availability zones within one region, protecting against a datacenter-level failure without the latency or cost of replicating to a second region entirely.
flashcards.detail: This sits between locally-redundant storage (protects against a single rack/disk failure only) and the cross-region options covered under availability zones vs. paired (secondary) regions.

flashcards.back: Defining infrastructure in declarative template files (ARM, Bicep, or Terraform) that can be version-controlled, reviewed, and deployed repeatably, instead of manually clicking through the Azure portal.
flashcards.detail: A design requirement for consistent, repeatable, auditable deployments across multiple environments is a strong signal that IaC belongs in the answer, not manual provisioning.

flashcards.back: Combines zone-redundant storage (ZRS) synchronous replication within the primary region with asynchronous replication to a second, paired region — protecting against both a zone failure and a full regional outage in one redundancy setting.
flashcards.detail: This is the strongest option among storage redundancy: LRS, ZRS, GRS, and GZRS for a design that must survive a regional outage without sacrificing the zone-level durability ZRS already provides day to day.

flashcards.back: The configuration on an Azure resource that routes its platform logs and metrics to a destination — a Log Analytics workspace, storage account, or Event Hub — since resource logs aren't collected anywhere by default until a diagnostic setting sends them there.
flashcards.detail: This is the piece a design is missing if Azure Monitor Metrics vs. Logs mentions a log type that never seems to show up anywhere — the resource-level diagnostic setting to actually emit it hasn't been configured.

flashcards.front: Bicep and ARM templates for landing zone deployment
flashcards.back: Enterprise-scale landing zones are deployed and updated as Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — Bicep or ARM templates, sometimes Terraform — rather than clicked together in the portal, so the same governed baseline (Azure landing zones) can be redeployed consistently across subscriptions and re-applied whenever the reference architecture changes.
flashcards.detail: Treating a landing zone's own definition as IaC means a change to policy or hub networking gets tested and versioned like any other code change, instead of being a one-off manual edit to a subscription that already exists.

flashcards.back: Azure Advisor analyzes your actual resource configuration and usage telemetry, then generates personalized recommendations organized by the same five pillars as the Azure Well-Architected Framework — reliability, security, cost, operational excellence, and performance.
flashcards.detail: Advisor's recommendations are specific to what's actually deployed and how it's being used, unlike the Azure Well-Architected Framework's pillars themselves, which are general design guidance applied before or during a build.

flashcards.back: Resource Graph queries resource metadata (type, location, tags, configuration) across many subscriptions at once using a Kusto-like query language, letting an architect audit governance and compliance for management groups, subscriptions, and resource groups without opening each one individually in the portal.
flashcards.detail: This is read-only inventory and querying — Azure Policy is still the tool that actually enforces or remediates what Resource Graph merely reports on.

flashcards.back: Network Watcher provides network-level diagnostic tools — IP flow verify (is a specific rule allowing or blocking a flow), NSG flow logs (a record of every evaluated flow), and Connection Troubleshoot (an end-to-end reachability test) — for troubleshooting connectivity issues after a network is already built.
flashcards.detail: These are diagnostic tools for an existing network, not design-time governance controls — Azure landing zones and Azure Policy govern how a network gets built and configured in the first place.

flashcards.back: A managed service that provides browser-based RDP or SSH access to a VM through the Azure portal over TLS, without ever requiring a public IP address on the target VM itself. Bastion must be deployed into a dedicated AzureBastionSubnet within a VNet — commonly the hub VNet in a hub-and-spoke network topology — and it's a complementary layer, not a replacement, for the network security group (NSG) vs. Azure Firewall filtering that still protects those same VMs.
flashcards.detail: Removing the VM's public IP closes one attack surface, but it doesn't make NSG rules optional — layered defense still applies with Bastion in place, not instead of it.

flashcards.back: A rule-based policy on a storage account that automatically moves blobs between access tiers: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive as they age, and deletes them once a defined retention period ends, all without anyone manually re-tiering or cleaning up data by hand. This is what actually enforces a cost-driven access-tier strategy over time, rather than a one-time manual tier assignment made only at upload.
flashcards.detail: A lifecycle policy is what actually delivers on the cost promise of Archive tier in practice — without one, data that should have aged into a cheaper tier months ago just sits in Hot, quietly costing more than it needs to.

flashcards.back: A shorthand for the range of ways a workload can move to the cloud, from least to most change: Rehost (lift-and-shift, minimal change), Refactor/re-platform (small optimizations, like moving to a managed database), Rearchitect (redesign for cloud-native scale), Rebuild (start over cloud-native), and Retire (decommission it instead of moving it at all). Azure Migrate is the tool that typically drives the discovery and assessment deciding which of these five paths actually fits a given workload.
flashcards.detail: A design question that only ever considers Rehost is missing the point of the framework — the 5 R's exist specifically because different workloads justify different amounts of change, and picking the same strategy for everything usually means either overpaying for cloud-native rework nobody needed, or under-investing in a workload that would have benefited from it.

flashcards.back: A system-assigned managed identity is created and tied to the lifecycle of a single resource, deleted automatically when that resource is deleted, and can't be referenced or shared by another resource. A user-assigned managed identity is created as its own standalone resource, can be assigned to many resources at once, and persists independently of any one resource's lifecycle.
flashcards.detail: A pattern where several VMs or Function Apps all need to authenticate as the same identity to a downstream resource points to a single user-assigned managed identity, not a separate system-assigned identity configured on each one.

flashcards.back: An initiative groups multiple individual policy definitions into a single assignable unit with a shared set of parameters, so an organization can assign, track compliance for, and manage many related policies — such as tagging, allowed resource types, and encryption requirements — together instead of as separate assignments. An initiative can bundle policies using any of the effects described in Azure Policy effects: Deny, Audit, and DeployIfNotExists into one assignable set.
flashcards.detail: Built-in initiatives are commonly what actually get assigned at a management group scope, so a whole bundled set of controls applies consistently to every subscription underneath, rather than assigning 15 separate policies by hand to each one.

flashcards.back: A small number of cloud-only, non-federated accounts with strong credentials, deliberately excluded from Conditional Access policies and closely monitored, kept specifically so an administrator can still sign in if a Conditional Access misconfiguration or an MFA outage locks everyone else out. These accounts are the deliberate exception carved out of every Conditional Access vs. multifactor authentication (MFA) policy in the tenant.
flashcards.detail: Excluding these accounts from Conditional Access isn't a security gap — it's the one deliberate exception that keeps the whole tenant from being permanently locked out by its own policies.

flashcards.front: Cosmos DB APIs: Core (SQL), MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, and Table
flashcards.back: Cosmos DB is a multi-model service, and the API chosen determines the data model and drivers an application uses: Core (SQL) for native JSON documents with SQL-like queries, MongoDB for wire-protocol compatibility with existing MongoDB apps, Cassandra for existing Cassandra workloads, Gremlin for graph data and traversal queries, and Table for a premium, higher-scale replacement for Azure Table storage. Cosmos DB consistency levels and Cosmos DB partition key design apply the same way no matter which API is chosen.
flashcards.detail: Picking the API isn't just a syntax preference — it's what lets an existing MongoDB or Cassandra application move to Cosmos DB with minimal code changes, since the wire protocol stays compatible.

flashcards.front: Azure Database for PostgreSQL / MySQL Flexible Server
flashcards.back: Fully managed, open-source relational database hosting with built-in high availability (zone-redundant or same-zone), granular control over maintenance windows, and lower cost than the older single-server deployment option it has largely superseded. This sits alongside Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on a VM as the equivalent hosting choice for open-source engines instead of SQL Server.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario needs to migrate an existing PostgreSQL or MySQL application to Azure while keeping the same open-source engine, rather than rewriting it against Azure SQL Database or Cosmos DB.

flashcards.back: A time-based immutability policy enforces write-once, read-many (WORM) protection on blobs, preventing modification or deletion until a set retention period elapses. In locked mode, not even an account administrator can shorten the retention period or remove the policy before it expires. This is a stronger, prevention-based guarantee than a Blob storage lifecycle management policy, which only automates tiering and deletion over time rather than blocking either outright.
flashcards.detail: A regulatory requirement that data be genuinely undeletable until a retention period ends calls for a locked immutability policy specifically, not just soft delete, which still permits eventual deletion.

flashcards.front: Azure Synapse Analytics: serverless vs. dedicated SQL pools
flashcards.back: A serverless SQL pool bills per query based on the data actually processed, with no compute to provision or pay for while idle, suited to ad hoc or unpredictable querying. A dedicated SQL pool pre-allocates provisioned compute measured in DWUs, suited to sustained, predictable, high-performance workloads. Serverless pools commonly query files sitting directly in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 without first loading them into a database.
flashcards.detail: Choosing dedicated for infrequent, ad hoc analytics means paying for idle provisioned compute; choosing serverless for a constant, heavy workload can end up costing more per query than a dedicated pool would have.

flashcards.front: Availability sets: fault domains and update domains
flashcards.back: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (separate physical racks with independent power and network, protecting against hardware failure) and update domains (groups that Azure patches and reboots at different times, protecting against planned maintenance), all within a single datacenter. This operates at a narrower scope than Availability zones vs. paired (secondary) regions — protecting against rack-level and maintenance-level failure inside one datacenter, not the loss of the datacenter itself.
flashcards.detail: An availability set is the lighter-weight, single-datacenter alternative to spreading VMs across availability zones, worth reaching for when a scenario explicitly doesn't need datacenter-level protection.

flashcards.back: When a workload chains multiple dependent Azure services together, its overall availability is the product of each service's individual SLA, not the lowest single SLA in the chain — combining two services each rated at 99.9% actually yields a composite SLA below 99.9%, unless a redundant path is added to compensate. This is a concrete, calculable input to the reliability pillar of the Azure Well-Architected Framework, not just an abstract design goal.
flashcards.detail: This is why a design with several chained dependencies often needs redundant paths through some of those services — otherwise the composite math can quietly fall short of a stated availability target even when every individual service meets its own SLA.

flashcards.back: A common backup retention design that keeps daily backups (son) for a short window, weekly backups (father) for a medium window, and monthly or yearly backups (grandfather) for the longest window, balancing storage cost against how far back a restore point needs to reach. This retention design is configured on an Azure Backup policy, the same service covered in Azure Backup vs. Azure Site Recovery, not on Site Recovery's replication settings.
flashcards.detail: Azure Backup policies implement this by letting daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly retention rules be configured independently on the same policy, rather than keeping every daily recovery point forever.

flashcards.back: Spins up recovered VMs in an isolated network specifically to validate that replicated data is recoverable, without touching production traffic or the live replication itself. This is a feature of Azure Site Recovery specifically, the same service covered in Azure Backup vs. Azure Site Recovery, not of Azure Backup.
flashcards.detail: Running the test into an isolated virtual network, not the production VNet, avoids IP address and naming conflicts with the still-running primary VMs during the drill.

flashcards.front: Azure DNS: public zones vs. Private DNS zones
flashcards.back: A public DNS zone hosts a domain's records for internet-wide resolution. A Private DNS zone resolves names only within one or more linked virtual networks, commonly used to give a private endpoint a friendly name that still resolves to its private IP address instead of its public one. This is the missing piece referenced under Private endpoint vs. service endpoint: without a linked Private DNS zone, a private endpoint's normal hostname won't automatically resolve to its private IP address.
flashcards.detail: A private endpoint needs a linked Private DNS zone to make its private IP resolve automatically for VNet-based clients — without one, an application would have to be reconfigured to use the private endpoint's raw IP address directly.

flashcards.back: Provides outbound-only internet connectivity for resources in a subnet through a shared set of static public IP addresses, avoiding the SNAT port exhaustion that can occur behind a Standard Load Balancer's outbound rules under heavy outbound connection volume.
flashcards.detail: This solves outbound connectivity specifically — it doesn't provide any inbound path, which is a separate concern handled by a load balancer, Application Gateway, or Front Door.

flashcards.front: Managed disks: Standard SSD vs. Premium SSD vs. Ultra Disk
flashcards.back: Standard SSD suits dev/test or lighter, latency-tolerant workloads. Premium SSD targets production workloads needing consistent low latency and high IOPS, such as databases. Ultra Disk allows IOPS and throughput to be tuned independently of disk size, for the most demanding, latency-sensitive workloads.
flashcards.detail: A requirement to adjust IOPS or throughput on the fly, independent of how much disk capacity is provisioned, is the specific signal for Ultra Disk over Premium SSD.

flashcards.back: Manages a group of identical, load-balanced VMs as a single resource, automatically adding or removing instances based on autoscale rules — the VM-based equivalent of scaling out an App Service plan, but for IaaS workloads that need full OS control. Depending on how it's configured, a scale set's instances can be spread across Availability sets: fault domains and update domains within one datacenter, or across multiple availability zones.
flashcards.detail: Combining autoscaling with either of those resiliency layouts means a scale set can absorb both a traffic spike and a rack- or zone-level failure without any manual intervention.

flashcards.front: Azure SQL Database purchasing models: DTU vs. vCore, and Hyperscale
flashcards.back: The DTU-based model bundles compute, memory, and storage I/O into a single blended unit, simple to budget but hard to scale any one dimension independently. The vCore model prices compute and storage separately, maps directly to physical cores and memory (easing on-premises core-license comparisons), and is the only model that offers the Hyperscale service tier, which can scale storage into the tens of terabytes with near-instant backups and fast scale-out using read replicas.
flashcards.detail: Hyperscale decouples storage growth from compute size entirely, which is the detail that matters when a scenario describes a database that needs to grow far beyond what a fixed DTU tier or a General Purpose/Business Critical vCore tier can comfortably hold.

flashcards.front: Cosmos DB throughput: provisioned vs. serverless capacity mode
flashcards.back: Provisioned throughput (standard or autoscale) reserves RU/s capacity ahead of time so performance is predictable, suited to steady or predictable workloads. Serverless capacity mode bills per request unit actually consumed, with no RU/s to provision or pay for while idle, suited to spiky or low-traffic workloads where paying for always-on capacity would waste money.
flashcards.detail: Autoscale, within provisioned mode, still reserves a maximum RU/s ceiling and scales automatically between a floor and that ceiling; serverless goes further and removes the need to provision any RU/s at all, but it caps total storage per container and isn't available alongside multi-region writes.

flashcards.front: Azure Data Factory vs. Synapse pipelines for data integration
flashcards.back: Azure Data Factory is a standalone, code-free ETL/ELT orchestration service for moving and transforming data across on-premises and cloud sources with a large library of connectors. Synapse pipelines provide that same underlying pipeline engine and designer experience, but built directly inside Azure Synapse Analytics, alongside Azure Synapse Analytics: serverless vs. dedicated SQL pools and Spark pools in one unified workspace.
flashcards.detail: Choosing Synapse pipelines over a standalone Data Factory instance is mainly about workspace consolidation — keeping ingestion, transformation, and querying together in one Synapse workspace — rather than a difference in the underlying orchestration capability itself.

flashcards.back: Lets a managing tenant, such as a managed service provider or a central IT organization, administer resources in one or more customer tenants directly, through delegated Azure RBAC roles, without the customer's resources ever leaving their own tenant and without the managing tenant needing a separate guest account in each one.
flashcards.detail: This is the design answer whenever a scenario describes a single team centrally managing resources across multiple, separate Entra ID tenants — Azure Lighthouse delegates access across tenant boundaries, something management groups and plain Azure RBAC can't do on their own, since both are scoped to a single tenant.

flashcards.front: Custom RBAC roles: Actions, NotActions, and DataActions
flashcards.back: A custom role definition grants permissions through Actions, the control-plane operations it allows, and can carve out exceptions with NotActions, operations explicitly excluded from what Actions already grants. Data-plane access — reading or writing the data inside a resource, like a blob or a queue message — is governed separately through DataActions, which Actions and NotActions never cover.
flashcards.detail: A built-in role like Reader can't be edited directly, so a requirement for a role just slightly narrower or broader than any built-in one — including some data-plane access that no existing built-in role quite matches — is the exam's signal to design a custom role instead.

flashcards.back: A cloud security posture management (CSPM) and workload protection platform that continuously assesses resource configuration against security benchmarks, produces a Secure Score to track improvement over time, and can enable workload-specific threat protection for servers, storage, databases, and more, for active threat detection that goes beyond configuration assessment alone.
flashcards.detail: Secure Score is a continuously recalculated posture metric derived from actual configuration, which makes it a different kind of signal than Azure Advisor's recommendations — Advisor spans all five Well-Architected pillars, while Defender for Cloud's score is specifically a security-posture measurement.

flashcards.back: A fault-injection testing service that deliberately triggers failures — killing a VM, injecting network latency, throttling a dependency — against a running Azure environment, so a team can observe and validate how a workload's actual resiliency design behaves under real failure conditions, rather than only on paper.
flashcards.detail: This complements, rather than replaces, Azure Site Recovery test failover: Chaos Studio validates how a live, running architecture tolerates and recovers from in-place faults, while a Site Recovery test failover specifically validates that replicated data in a secondary location is recoverable.

flashcards.front: Cosmos DB multi-region failover priority and write-conflict resolution
flashcards.back: With multiple read regions configured, an account's failover priority list determines which region Cosmos DB promotes to primary if the current write region fails, and automatic failover follows that list without manual intervention unless it's disabled. If multi-region writes are enabled instead, concurrent writes to the same item in different regions are resolved automatically, by last-writer-wins based on a timestamp, unless a custom conflict resolution policy is defined.
flashcards.detail: A requirement that conflicting writes be resolved by specific business logic, rather than simply keeping whichever write has the latest timestamp, is the signal to configure a custom conflict resolution policy instead of relying on the default last-writer-wins behavior.

flashcards.back: Lets an administrator manually trigger an unplanned failover of a GRS, GZRS, RA-GRS, or RA-GZRS storage account, promoting the secondary region to primary during a real outage. After the failover, the account temporarily becomes locally redundant in the new primary region until geo-redundancy is explicitly reconfigured, and any writes that hadn't yet replicated to the secondary before the failover are lost.
flashcards.detail: This is a deliberate, administrator-triggered action for a genuine regional outage, not something Azure performs automatically on its own — a design that assumes failover happens by itself without anyone initiating it is assuming a behavior the feature doesn't actually provide.

flashcards.front: Azure Site Recovery recovery points: app-consistent vs. crash-consistent
flashcards.back: A crash-consistent recovery point captures disk data as if the VM had simply lost power, with no guarantee that in-memory or in-flight application transactions were flushed to disk first. An app-consistent recovery point additionally quiesces the application before the snapshot, guaranteeing that in-flight transactions are captured cleanly, at the cost of being taken less frequently than crash-consistent points.
flashcards.detail: A database workload that can't tolerate a failover point that might land mid-transaction is the scenario that calls for app-consistent recovery points specifically, even though they're captured on a longer interval than crash-consistent points.

flashcards.front: Traffic Manager routing methods: Priority, Weighted, Performance, and Geographic
flashcards.back: Priority routing sends all traffic to the highest-priority healthy endpoint, falling back to the next one only on failure — the method that actually implements an active-passive multi-region design at the DNS layer. Weighted distributes traffic across endpoints by a configured ratio, useful for a gradual rollout. Performance routes to whichever endpoint has the lowest network latency for the requester. Geographic routes based on the requester's geographic location, often to satisfy data-residency requirements.
flashcards.detail: Picking Priority for what's actually meant to be an active-active multi-region design would quietly turn the backup regions into idle, untested capacity — Performance or Weighted across every region is what an active-active design actually calls for at the DNS layer.

flashcards.back: Extends Azure management — Azure Policy, RBAC, Azure Monitor, and tagging — to servers, Kubernetes clusters, and other infrastructure running outside Azure entirely: on-premises, at the edge, or in another cloud, by projecting each one as an Azure resource without migrating the underlying workload itself.
flashcards.detail: A requirement to apply the same governance and monitoring tooling to on-premises servers that an organization already applies to its native Azure VMs, without actually moving those servers into Azure, is the signal for Azure Arc rather than a migration tool like Azure Migrate.

flashcards.front: Azure Private Link service vs. private endpoint
flashcards.back: A private endpoint, covered under Private endpoint vs. service endpoint, is how a consumer privately reaches an existing PaaS resource. Azure Private Link service is the other side of that same mechanism: it lets an organization publish its own service, running behind a Standard Load Balancer, so that other VNets, or even other tenants, can connect to it through a private endpoint of their own, without that traffic ever crossing the public internet.
flashcards.detail: A scenario about privately consuming someone else's PaaS resource needs a private endpoint; a scenario about an organization privately exposing its own custom service to outside consumers needs Private Link service on the provider's side.

flashcards.front: API Management network integration: external vs. internal VNet modes
flashcards.back: In external mode, Azure API Management's gateway, developer portal, and management endpoints get a public IP, while the backends it calls can still sit privately inside a VNet. In internal mode, every one of those endpoints, including the gateway itself, only gets a private IP inside the VNet, so APIs are reachable only from within that network or something connected to it, with no public endpoint existing at all.
flashcards.detail: A requirement that an API only ever be reachable from inside the corporate network or over ExpressRoute, never from the public internet, is the signal for internal VNet mode specifically, not just locking down the backend behind the gateway.

flashcards.front: Load Balancer SKUs: Basic vs. Standard
flashcards.back: The Basic SKU has no SLA, no zone redundancy, no outbound rules of its own, and is open by default, allowing inbound traffic even with no NSG attached. The Standard SKU adds a 99.99% SLA, supports a zone-redundant frontend IP, provides explicit outbound rules to manage SNAT port allocation, and is secure by default, blocking all inbound traffic unless an NSG explicitly allows it.
flashcards.detail: That last difference catches teams off guard migrating from Basic to Standard: VMs that were reachable with no NSG at all under Basic suddenly become unreachable under Standard until an explicit allow rule is added, since Standard assumes nothing is allowed until an NSG says otherwise.

questions.question: Fabrikam's security policy forbids storing passwords, or hashes of passwords, in the cloud, and the team will not build federation infrastructure. Sign-in to Entra ID applications must keep working if any single on-premises server fails. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Pass-through authentication, with agents installed on multiple domain-joined hosts
AD FS federation, with two federation servers behind a load balancer
Password hash synchronization, with a second Entra Connect server in staging mode
Pass-through authentication, with one agent on the Microsoft Entra Connect server
questions.explanation: Pass-through authentication validates each password against on-premises AD, so no password or hash is stored in the cloud and no federation farm is needed. Because sign-in fails when no agent is reachable, installing agents on more than one host removes the single point of failure. A single agent meets the password rule but fails the "any single server" requirement. Password hash synchronization stores a hash of the on-premises password hash in Entra ID, which the policy forbids, and a staging-mode server does not change that. AD FS keeps passwords on premises but is exactly the federation infrastructure the team refuses to build.

questions.question: Contoso's 25 administrators permanently hold Global Administrator or subscription Owner. Auditors want privileged access to be time-limited, justified, and approved, with MFA required at the moment of use. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Replace the roles with narrower custom roles at management group scope
Convert the permanent assignments to eligible assignments in PIM
Enable a sign-in risk policy for administrator accounts
Require approval, justification, and MFA in the PIM role settings
Run a monthly access review of the permanent assignments
questions.explanation: Eligible assignments remove standing access, and the PIM role settings enforce approval, justification, and MFA at activation with a bounded duration; together they meet every audit requirement. A monthly access review only recertifies standing assignments, so the access stays standing between reviews. Narrower custom roles change what is permitted, not when or for how long. A sign-in risk policy reacts to suspicious sign-ins and neither time-limits nor approves privileged elevation.

questions.question: A policy assigned at a management group must make sure every storage account has a diagnostic setting that sends logs to a central workspace. Teams create accounts constantly, creation must never be blocked, and a diagnostic setting is a separate resource from the storage account. Which effect should the policy use?
options: DeployIfNotExists
Modify
Append
AuditIfNotExists
questions.explanation: DeployIfNotExists looks for a related resource, here the diagnostic setting, and deploys it when it is missing, without blocking creation of the storage account. AuditIfNotExists performs the same related-resource check but only reports noncompliance; nothing gets deployed. Modify and Append change properties or tags on the resource being evaluated and cannot create a separate resource. Accounts that were already noncompliant before the assignment are corrected by running a remediation task.

questions.question: A conglomerate has three subsidiaries, each with several subscriptions and its own IT team managing its own policies and RBAC. The parent company must enforce one mandatory tagging policy on every subscription, assigned once, and subsidiary teams must not be able to remove it. Which structure should you recommend?
options: A separate Entra tenant per subsidiary, with the tagging policy assigned in each tenant
A parent management group with a child group per subsidiary, assigning the tagging policy at the parent
All subscriptions directly under the tenant root group, with the tagging policy assigned to each subscription
A management group per subsidiary, with the tagging policy assigned separately to each one
questions.explanation: A policy assigned at the parent management group is created once, inherited by every child group and subscription, and cannot be removed by subsidiary administrators who have no rights at the parent scope, while each child group still holds that subsidiary's own policies and RBAC. Assigning the policy separately per child group repeats the work and leaves each subsidiary's owners able to delete their own copy. Subscriptions directly under the root also need one assignment each and give no subsidiary-level grouping. Separate tenants multiply identity administration, and a policy assignment cannot span tenants.
questions.whyTested: Management-group inheritance is the mechanism that delivers 'enforced once from above, independent below'. Each wrong answer sounds organized but repeats the assignment, loses the subsidiary grouping, or fragments the tenant, so the exam is checking whether you pick the structure that actually inherits rather than the one that merely looks tidy.

questions.question: A healthcare group monitors everything through one Log Analytics workspace in East US. Its German clinical subsidiary must keep log data inside Germany, control its own access and retention, and still run its own KQL queries and alerts. How should you change the design?
options: Send the subsidiary's logs to a storage account in Germany through a diagnostic setting
Keep the single workspace and restrict the subsidiary's tables with table-level access control
Keep the single workspace and set a longer retention period on the subsidiary's tables
Create a workspace in Germany West Central for the subsidiary and keep the central one for the rest
questions.explanation: A workspace is bound to one region, so only a dedicated workspace in a German region keeps the data in Germany; it carries its own access and retention settings, and the subsidiary can query and alert on it directly. Table-level access control in the shared workspace still stores the data in East US. A longer table retention changes how long data stays, not where it lives. Archiving to a German storage account satisfies residency but gives up the interactive queries and alerts the subsidiary needs.

questions.question: Contractors from partner firms request access themselves to three applications and a SharePoint site for the length of their contract. A manager must approve each request, and the access must be removed on the contract end date without anyone revoking it by hand. Which Entra ID Governance feature fits?
options: A dynamic group whose membership rule checks a contractor attribute
A recurring access review with results applied automatically
An entitlement management access package with an expiration date
PIM eligible assignments with a fixed end date
questions.explanation: An access package bundles the applications and site, supports a request-and-approval workflow, and its assignments expire on their own. A recurring access review can remove access when its results are applied automatically, but it only runs on a schedule and offers no request, approval, or bundling. A dynamic group grants access while an attribute matches, with no approval step and no end date tied to the contract. PIM eligible assignments govern privileged roles, not application and site access for external users.

questions.question: Operations needs an alert within a minute when a VM's CPU stays above 90%. Security needs to join sign-in events, firewall logs, and VM events across six months of data. Which pairing of Azure Monitor capabilities fits?
options: An activity log alert for CPU; the Activity log for the joins
A metric alert rule on the CPU metric; KQL queries over a Log Analytics workspace
A metric alert for CPU; Metrics Explorer with dimension splitting for the joins
A log search alert on the Perf table for CPU; Metrics Explorer for the joins
questions.explanation: Platform metrics are lightweight numeric time series evaluated every minute, so a metric alert is the fast, cheap way to catch a CPU threshold, while joining several record types across months is exactly what Log Analytics and KQL do. A log search alert can watch CPU but adds ingestion and query latency, and Metrics Explorer cannot join record types. The Activity log records control-plane operations, not performance or security events. Splitting a metric by dimension is not a join, and platform metrics are kept for a limited period.

questions.question: Contoso is building its first enterprise Azure environment. Every new application subscription must start with the same management group placement, policies, RBAC, and a connection to a shared hub network, with no setup work by the application teams. Which approach should you recommend?
options: One shared subscription with a resource group per team and Azure Policy assigned to each group
A Bicep template that each application team runs to deploy a spoke VNet peered to the hub network
An Azure landing zone, with a platform connectivity subscription and new subscriptions created under governed management groups
A management group hierarchy with a policy initiative and RBAC roles assigned at the top level
questions.explanation: A landing zone packages all the pieces: a management group hierarchy carrying inherited policy and RBAC, platform subscriptions hosting the hub network and identity, and a repeatable way to place each new subscription into that structure so it starts governed and connected. A management group hierarchy with policy and RBAC covers governance but delivers no hub connectivity. A template that application teams run themselves covers networking only, depends on each team running it, and brings no governance inheritance. A shared subscription with per-team resource groups blurs billing and scale boundaries and has no new subscriptions to inherit anything.

questions.question: A financial firm is migrating an on-premises SQL Server instance with 12 databases that rely on SQL Agent jobs and cross-database queries. It wants Microsoft to own OS and engine patching and backups, and it will not rewrite the application. Which service should you recommend?
options: Azure SQL Managed Instance
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale
Azure SQL Database elastic pool
SQL Server on an Azure VM with automated patching
questions.explanation: Managed Instance offers near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility, including SQL Agent and cross-database queries, as fully managed PaaS where Microsoft handles OS patching, engine patching, and backups. An elastic pool shares resources among single databases that cannot run SQL Agent jobs or query across databases the way an instance can, and Hyperscale is a single-database service tier with the same limits. SQL Server on a VM with automated patching keeps the features, but the VM, its OS configuration, and its backups remain the customer's responsibility.

questions.question: A messaging app uses a Cosmos DB account with multi-region writes. A user must always see their own just-posted messages after reloading, reads of other users' messages may lag, and the team wants the lowest latency and RU cost that still gives that guarantee. Which consistency level fits?
options: Session
Bounded staleness
Strong
Eventual
questions.explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes and monotonic reads within a client session while staying low-latency and cheap, which is exactly the stated need. Eventual is cheaper still but can return a stale view that omits a user's own post. Bounded staleness limits how stale reads can be for all clients, a stronger and costlier guarantee than needed. Strong is not supported on accounts with multiple write regions, and even where it is available it costs the most latency and RUs.

questions.question: A Cosmos DB container stores IoT telemetry partitioned by deviceType, but 95% of devices share one type. Writes to that logical partition are throttled although most of the container's total RU/s goes unused. Dashboards almost always query one device's readings. What should you do?
options: Raise the container's maximum autoscale RU/s so each partition receives more throughput
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by the device identifier
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by deviceType combined with the datacenter region
Migrate the data to a container partitioned by the ingestion timestamp
questions.explanation: A partition key should have many distinct values and match the common query filter; the device identifier has high cardinality and lines up with per-device queries. A timestamp key is high-cardinality but monotonic, so every current write lands on the newest partition, which creates a different hot spot and scatters per-device queries across partitions. Combining deviceType with a region still yields only a handful of values, so the hot partition remains. More RU/s is divided among physical partitions, so the hot partition still hits its own per-partition limit.

questions.question: A storage account must keep accepting writes without any failover if one datacenter in the primary region is lost. During a regional outage, a reporting app must be able to read the data from a second region without anyone initiating a failover. Which redundancy option should you select?
options: Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) without read access
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) in the primary region
Read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS)
questions.explanation: RA-GZRS keeps synchronous copies across three zones in the primary region, so losing a datacenter does not interrupt writes, and replicates asynchronously to a secondary region whose copy is readable at any time. RA-GRS keeps its primary-region copies in one datacenter, so losing it would interrupt writes until a failover. GZRS has the same zone resilience, but its secondary copy cannot be read until a failover occurs. ZRS has no secondary region at all.

questions.question: A legal team keeps seven years of contract records in Blob storage. Each record is opened once or twice a year, and when an attorney asks for one it must open immediately, with no restore step. Storage cost should be as low as possible within that constraint. Which access tier should you use?
options: Cold
Archive
Cool
Hot
questions.explanation: Cold is the lowest-cost tier that is still online, so blobs open immediately, and its higher read cost and 90-day minimum suit records opened once or twice a year. Archive is cheaper to store, but blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read, which can take hours and rules out immediate access. Cool is also online, but it costs more to store than Cold and is aimed at data accessed somewhat more often. Hot has the highest storage cost and is meant for frequently accessed data.

questions.question: A data engineering team runs Spark jobs over petabytes of semi-structured files. Each team needs ACLs at the directory and file level, and nightly jobs rename large folders, which must complete as a single atomic operation. Cost should stay low. Which storage solution fits?
options: Azure Files Premium with an NFS share mounted on each Spark node
Azure NetApp Files with a large capacity pool and snapshots
Blob storage with a flat namespace and RBAC assigned per container
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (a storage account with hierarchical namespace)
questions.explanation: ADLS Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace, which provides POSIX-style ACLs on directories and files and atomic directory renames at lake scale, at Blob pricing. A flat namespace has no real directories, so renaming a folder means copying and deleting every blob, and RBAC applies at container scope or above rather than per file. Premium Azure Files and Azure NetApp Files are higher-cost file-share services, not lake-scale analytics storage with ACLs.

questions.question: A team plans to move an on-premises SQL Server with 12 databases to Azure SQL Managed Instance, with minimal downtime at cutover. Which step should the team take FIRST?
options: Take full backups of every database and restore them to the target with native restore
Assess the source databases for compatibility blockers, for example with Data Migration Assistant
Provision a Managed Instance sized to match the source server's CPU and memory
Start an online migration in Database Migration Service and fix errors as they appear
questions.explanation: Assessment comes first because its findings decide whether Managed Instance is a viable target and how to size it; starting a migration before that risks discovering blockers in the middle of a cutover. Starting an online migration in DMS or restoring native backups are migration steps that follow once the target is validated. Provisioning a target to match source hardware guesses at size before real utilization and compatibility data exist.

questions.question: A three-tier VM application must be running in the paired region within one hour of a regional outage, losing no more than 15 minutes of data, with the tiers starting in the correct order. Which service should the design use?
options: Azure Backup with cross-region restore on a GRS vault
Disk snapshots copied to the paired region by a scheduled script
VMs spread across availability zones in the primary region
Azure Site Recovery replication with an ordered recovery plan
questions.explanation: Site Recovery continuously replicates the VMs to the paired region, giving an RPO of minutes, and a recovery plan starts the tiers in order, which meets both targets. Azure Backup with cross-region restore can restore into the paired region, but the RPO is the backup interval and restoring every VM takes far longer than failing over. Availability zones protect against datacenter loss, not a regional outage. Script-copied snapshots have no tier ordering or failover orchestration, and their RPO depends on the script schedule.

questions.question: A line-of-business VM application must stay online if a single datacenter in its region fails, and must be recoverable in another region, with up to 15 minutes of data loss, if the whole region is lost. Which design meets both requirements?
options: VMs in an availability set, replicated to a secondary region with Azure Site Recovery
VMs spread across availability zones, replicated to a secondary region with Azure Site Recovery
VMs spread across availability zones, backed up daily with Azure Backup to a GRS vault
VMs in one availability zone, replicated to a different zone in the same region with Azure Site Recovery
questions.explanation: Spreading the VMs across availability zones keeps the tier running when one datacenter fails, and Site Recovery replicates continuously to another region, giving an RPO of minutes if the whole region is lost. An availability set stays inside one datacenter, so losing that datacenter takes the tier down. A daily backup allows up to a day of data loss, far beyond 15 minutes. Zone-to-zone replication keeps the data in the same region, so a regional loss still takes everything down.

questions.question: An app uses 40 databases on one Azure SQL logical server and a fixed connection string. After a regional outage, all 40 databases must fail over together to a secondary region with no application change. What should you configure?
options: An auto-failover group, with the read-write listener endpoint in the connection string
Geo-restore of each database from geo-redundant backups into the secondary region
Zone-redundant configuration for each database in the primary region
Active geo-replication on each database, failing over each one individually
questions.explanation: An auto-failover group fails every database in the group over together and keeps the read-write listener endpoint stable, so the fixed connection string keeps working. Active geo-replication fails over per database, and each failover changes which server is primary, so connection strings would have to change or be managed database by database. Geo-restore rebuilds each database from backups on a different server, which takes much longer and also changes the server name. Zone redundancy only protects against a datacenter loss inside the primary region.

questions.question: A reporting application must be running again within 4 hours of a regional outage and lose no more than 15 minutes of data. The business wants the lowest cost that meets both targets. Which design should you choose?
options: Keep a hot standby copy of every VM running continuously in the secondary region, with manual failover
Replicate the VMs to the secondary region with Site Recovery, leaving recovery compute unprovisioned until a failover
Back up the VMs hourly to a GRS vault and restore them in the secondary region after an outage
Run the full application in both regions behind Front Door, with a globally replicated database
questions.explanation: Site Recovery replicates continuously, giving an RPO of minutes, and bills only for replication and storage until a failover starts the VMs; recovery within a few hours satisfies a 4-hour RTO, so this is the cheapest design that hits both numbers. Running everything in both regions is the fastest but by far the most expensive, and the RTO does not need it. Hourly backups meet the RTO but can lose up to an hour of data, missing the 15-minute RPO. A hot standby meets both targets but pays for full compute in the second region around the clock, which the cost requirement rules out.
questions.whyTested: This question shape pairs numeric RTO and RPO targets with a cost constraint, so several designs technically work and the skill being tested is picking the cheapest one that still satisfies both numbers, rather than the most resilient-sounding option or the one that merely mentions replication or backup.

questions.question: A global app must keep serving users with no failover delay when a region fails, and users must be able to write data in their nearest region. Which design meets both requirements?
options: Traffic Manager weighted routing to two regions, with an Azure SQL read replica in the second region
Front Door with priority routing to a standby region, with an Azure SQL auto-failover group
Front Door routing to two active regions, with a GRS-replicated storage account as the data tier
Front Door routing to two active regions, with a Cosmos DB account that has multi-region writes
questions.explanation: Front Door can send traffic to two active regions at once, and Cosmos DB with multi-region writes accepts writes in each region, so a regional failure simply removes one active region and no failover step is needed. Priority routing to a standby region with a failover group is active-passive, so recovery takes time. A read replica keeps a single writer, so users far from it still write across regions, and Traffic Manager adds DNS-cache delay. A GRS storage account accepts writes only in its primary region, so the data tier is not active-active.

questions.question: A team will run microservices as containers. They must scale on HTTP load and on queue length, including down to zero instances when idle, and they do not want to operate Kubernetes node pools or cluster upgrades. Which compute service fits?
options: Azure Container Instances container groups
Azure Kubernetes Service with the KEDA add-on
Azure Container Apps
Azure App Service with containers and autoscale rules
questions.explanation: Container Apps provides built-in HTTP and event-driven scaling, including scale to zero, with no cluster to manage. AKS with KEDA can scale the same way, but the team would still own node pools, upgrades, and cluster configuration. An App Service plan keeps at least one instance running, so it cannot scale to zero. Container Instances runs container groups with no autoscaler of its own.

questions.question: A queue-triggered job runs briefly a few times a day. The company wants no compute charge while the job is idle and no servers to manage. Which hosting option fits?
options: An App Service plan with Always On enabled
Azure Container Apps with a minimum of one replica
Azure Functions on a Premium plan with one pre-warmed instance
Azure Functions on a Consumption plan
questions.explanation: A Consumption plan bills per execution and scales to zero, so an idle job costs nothing. A Premium plan keeps at least one pre-warmed instance running and bills for it continuously. A Container Apps app with a minimum of one replica also pays for that replica while idle. An App Service plan is billed for its reserved instances whether or not any code runs.

questions.question: A dozen application teams each own a VNet in one region. All must reach a shared firewall, VPN gateway, and DNS service, but must not reach each other's VNets, and the team wants that isolation without adding custom routing. Which topology fits?
options: Full-mesh peering between all application VNets and the hub
Hub-and-spoke, with each application VNet peered only to the hub VNet
Virtual WAN, with every VNet connected to the hub's default route table
One shared VNet with a subnet and network security group per team
questions.explanation: Peering is non-transitive, so spokes peered only to the hub reach the shared services but cannot reach one another by default; no routing work is needed for isolation. In Virtual WAN, VNets connected to a hub's default route table can reach each other, so isolation would need custom route tables. Full-mesh peering creates direct spoke-to-spoke paths. A single shared VNet abandons the separate VNets each team owns and relies on NSG rules for isolation.

questions.question: A trading firm needs private, predictable-latency connectivity from its datacenter to Azure. The connection must survive an ExpressRoute path failure, the firm wants the lowest added cost, and a few minutes of higher latency during a failure are acceptable. What should you recommend?
options: A second ExpressRoute circuit at a different peering location
ExpressRoute Global Reach linking the datacenter to a second on-premises site
An active-active VPN gateway with two Site-to-Site tunnels over separate internet links
ExpressRoute as the primary path, with a Site-to-Site VPN configured as the failover path
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides the predictable private path, and a Site-to-Site VPN can coexist with it as a lower-cost backup that takes over if the circuit fails; the extra latency during a failover is acceptable here. A second circuit at another peering location is the most resilient design but adds the cost of a whole circuit, which the firm wants to avoid. Two VPN tunnels are resilient but give up the predictability of a private circuit entirely. Global Reach links on-premises sites to each other through the Microsoft backbone and does not add a backup path into Azure.

questions.question: A global retailer needs one entry point that sends users to the nearest healthy regional deployment, fails over in seconds rather than waiting on DNS caches, caches static content at the edge, and applies a single WAF policy to all regions. Which should you use?
options: Azure CDN in front of a Standard Load Balancer in each region
Azure Front Door with a global WAF policy
Azure Traffic Manager with an Application Gateway WAF in each region
A single regional Application Gateway v2 with autoscale and WAF
questions.explanation: Front Door is a global layer-7 entry point: it routes by latency and health at the edge with real data-plane failover, caches content at the edge, and enforces one WAF policy centrally. Traffic Manager only answers DNS queries, so failover is bounded by DNS TTL and client caching, and the WAF would have to be configured in every region. A single Application Gateway is regional. A CDN caches content but has no application-aware routing or WAF of its own, and a Standard Load Balancer works at layer 4 within one region.
questions.whyTested: Front Door, Traffic Manager, Application Gateway, and CDN-plus-load-balancer combinations get stacked together constantly because each solves part of the problem at a different layer and scope. This question tests whether you notice the requirement that only a global layer-7 data-path service meets: failover that does not depend on DNS caching, a single central WAF, and edge caching in one service.

questions.question: A hub-and-spoke network must limit workloads' outbound internet traffic to a list of approved domain names, some with wildcards, and log every allowed and denied connection centrally, without maintaining rules on each subnet. Which resource should you deploy in the hub?
options: A NAT gateway on each spoke subnet
Azure Firewall with application rules in a firewall policy
An Application Gateway with WAF in the hub
Network security groups on each spoke subnet that use service tags
questions.explanation: Azure Firewall application rules filter outbound traffic by FQDN, including wildcards, and its logs are centralized, all managed once in the hub. NSGs filter on IP address, port, and protocol, and service tags only name Microsoft-managed address ranges, so they cannot express arbitrary approved domains and would have to be maintained on every subnet. A NAT gateway provides outbound addresses and does no filtering. An Application Gateway with WAF protects inbound web traffic to your apps, not outbound traffic from workloads.

questions.question: Before migrating 400 on-premises VMs, a team must discover them, map which servers communicate with each other so they can be moved in dependent groups, and get right-sized Azure VM recommendations from actual utilization. Which should anchor this phase?
options: Azure Migrate: Server Migration, replicating the VMs to Azure
Azure Migrate discovery and assessment with dependency analysis
Azure Advisor recommendations for the subscription the VMs will land in
The Azure TCO Calculator, using server counts and sizes entered by hand
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate's discovery and assessment collects configuration and performance data from the on-premises VMs, recommends right-sized Azure VMs and costs, and its dependency analysis shows server-to-server connections so related servers move together. The TCO Calculator works from numbers someone types in, so it discovers nothing and cannot see utilization or dependencies. Server Migration is the replication and cutover tool used after assessment. Advisor analyzes resources that are already running in Azure.

questions.question: An order system must process each customer's orders strictly in the sequence submitted, discard duplicate submissions, and set poison messages aside for review. Which service should it use?
options: Azure Event Hubs with the customer ID as the partition key
Azure Event Grid with an event subscription per customer
An Azure Service Bus queue with sessions enabled
Azure Storage queues with a visibility timeout
questions.explanation: Service Bus sessions give first-in-first-out processing per customer, duplicate detection discards repeats, and the dead-letter queue sets poison messages aside. Storage queues offer no FIFO guarantee or built-in duplicate detection. Event Hubs keeps order within a partition, but it is a streaming ingestion service with no dead-lettering or duplicate detection. Event Grid pushes discrete event notifications and does not provide ordered queue processing.

questions.question: A company exposes backend APIs hosted on VMs, App Service, and AKS to external partners. Each partner needs its own subscription key and rate limit, and some responses must be transformed from XML to JSON. Which service should sit in front of the backends?
options: Azure Front Door with a rules engine
Azure Logic Apps with an HTTP trigger
Azure Application Gateway with path-based routing rules
Azure API Management with products and policies
questions.explanation: API Management fronts any backend with per-consumer subscriptions and keys, rate limits and quotas, and policies that transform requests and responses, plus versioning and a developer portal. Application Gateway and Front Door can route by path to different backends, but they do not issue per-partner keys, enforce per-consumer quotas, or transform payloads as an API product. Logic Apps can be made to behave like an API, but it is a workflow engine, not an API gateway.

questions.question: An integration team must connect a SaaS CRM, an on-premises ERP through a data gateway, and SharePoint.
