Pass-through authentication instead validates every sign-in against on-premises Active Directory in real time through a lightweight agent, which means no password data is ever stored in the cloud, but it also means sign-in stops working if every authentication agent happens to be offline at once. Federation goes further still, handing authentication off entirely to an on-premises identity provider such as AD FS — useful when an organization has authentication requirements Entra ID can't satisfy on its own, at the cost of taking on and operating that federation infrastructure.

Once someone is authenticated, Conditional Access decides the conditions under which they're actually allowed to sign in — evaluating signals like the user, their device, their location, and a calculated risk score, then responding with a control. MFA is one of the controls Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy engine sitting next to it — a well-designed set of Conditional Access policies might require MFA only for risky sign-ins or unmanaged devices, rather than for absolutely everyone regardless of context. Because a Conditional Access misconfiguration could lock out every administrator at once, well-designed tenants also keep a small, tightly monitored emergency-access account deliberately excluded from those same Conditional Access policies — not a security hole, but the one guaranteed way in if the main policies ever misfire.

Even with strong sign-in and Conditional Access controls in place, most organizations still don't want administrators walking around with permanent, standing access to privileged roles. Privileged Identity Management (PIM) solves that by making privileged role membership something you activate — just-in-time and time-bound, optionally requiring approval and a written justification — rather than something that sits active on an account all day, every day, whether or not it's actually being used. PIM and Conditional Access are commonly layered together, such as requiring MFA (a Conditional Access control) as a condition of actually activating a PIM-eligible role.

Standing access outside of privileged roles gets managed differently, and this is a common point of confusion on the exam. Access reviews periodically recertify access that already exists — an administrator, or the resource owner themselves, is prompted to confirm someone still needs what they already have, or to revoke it. Entitlement management works earlier in that lifecycle: it bundles resources into requestable access packages with an approval workflow and, critically, built-in automatic expiration for newly granted access. A scenario about giving contractors bundled, time-boxed access to a defined set of resources is describing entitlement management; a scenario about periodically re-certifying access someone already holds is describing access reviews.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to hybrid identity design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
Think of the three sign-in options like three ways a branch office checks a visitor's identity against headquarters. Password hash sync is like the branch keeping its own up-to-date copy of the approved-visitor list, so it can approve a visitor instantly even if the phone line to headquarters is briefly down. Pass-through authentication is like the branch calling headquarters for every single visitor in real time — nothing is stored locally, but the branch is stuck if that phone line ever goes fully dead. Federation is like refusing to keep any list at all and always redirecting the visitor to headquarters' own front desk to be checked in directly.

PIM works like a fire extinguisher kept in a locked cabinet: a powerful tool, but not just left lying on a table for anyone to pick up whenever — you break the glass, note why you're using it, and it goes right back afterward instead of staying in your hands indefinitely.
commonTraps: Pass-through authentication still calls back to on-premises Active Directory for every sign-in — it needs at least one authentication agent online, unlike password hash sync, which keeps working through a brief on-premises outage.

MFA is a control Conditional Access can enforce, not a separate policy system — a scenario needing MFA only under certain conditions is a Conditional Access design question, not a standalone MFA setting.
Privileged Identity Management doesn't replace Conditional Access — the two are commonly layered, such as requiring MFA to activate a PIM-eligible role.

A scenario about time-boxed, bundled access for contractors or a project team points to entitlement management; a scenario about periodically re-certifying access that already exists points to access reviews.
lessons.scenario: A multinational retailer has an on-premises Active Directory it isn't ready to retire, but wants Entra ID sign-in to survive a brief outage of its on-premises network. It deploys password hash sync rather than pass-through authentication, so authentication can complete entirely in Entra ID if the on-premises link drops. For its cloud administrators, it layers Conditional Access (requiring MFA and a compliant device) with Privileged Identity Management, so no one holds standing access to a privileged role, and activating one still has to satisfy that same Conditional Access policy. A small, tightly monitored emergency-access account is deliberately excluded from that policy, so a misconfiguration can never lock every administrator out at once. Finally, its quarterly compliance process uses access reviews to recertify who still needs standing subscription-level access, while a separate entitlement management access package handles the shorter-lived access each new contractor team needs for the length of their engagement.
lessons.onTheJob: In design review, the sign-in method conversation is really a negotiation about who owns risk during an outage — a client that's been burned by a WAN failure before will fight hard for password hash sync even when the security team's slide deck favors federation for its 'zero cloud password' feel. PIM sounds like pure security hygiene until an architect has to sell it to admins who've had standing access for a decade and treat activating a role every time as a productivity tax, so the real work is scoping which roles genuinely need it instead of adding friction nobody asked for. Access reviews and entitlement management rarely get built pre-emptively — they usually get retrofitted after an audit finding, which means the design that looks over-engineered in year one often looks exactly right by year three.

lessons.title: Governance, Policy & Monitoring at Scale
lessons.summary: Management groups and Azure Policy, landing zones and adoption frameworks, and designing Log Analytics and Azure Monitor for an enterprise.
lessons.reading:
At the largest scale, Azure's resource hierarchy exists so governance can be set once and inherit downward instead of being repeated everywhere. Management groups sit above subscriptions, letting an organization apply a single Azure Policy assignment or RBAC role once at the top and have it flow down to every subscription, resource group, and resource underneath — a conglomerate with independently run subsidiaries can still give each one its own policy and RBAC boundary at the subscription level while sharing a small set of mandatory controls, like required tags, applied once at a shared management group above them all. Azure Policy itself has several effects worth telling apart: Deny blocks a noncompliant resource from being created or updated at all; Audit flags noncompliant resources for visibility without blocking anything; and DeployIfNotExists actively remediates by deploying something like a missing diagnostic setting whenever a required one isn't already there. Only DeployIfNotExists reaches back and fixes resources that are already noncompliant — Audit only reports on them, and Deny only stops new ones.

Rather than building this governance structure by hand for every new environment, Azure landing zones give an organization a pre-provisioned, consistent starting point — the management group hierarchy, policy assignments, identity foundations, and hub networking already built, so every new subscription lands into a governed environment from day one instead of each team configuring governance independently. Landing zones are the concrete, deployable implementation of the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF), Microsoft's broader methodology for an organization's whole cloud journey — strategy, readiness, adoption, governance, and ongoing management. Where CAF and landing zones shape how an environment gets built, the Azure Well-Architected Framework shapes how any individual workload's design gets evaluated afterward, across five pillars: reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency. A lot of AZ-305 scenario questions are really asking which of those five pillars a particular requirement is prioritizing, since a design can rarely maximize all five pillars at once.

Monitoring an environment this size raises its own design question: whether to centralize every resource's telemetry into one Log Analytics workspace, or split it across several decentralized workspaces per team or subscription. A centralized workspace makes cross-resource queries and overall cost visibility simple, but gives everyone sharing it a coarser access boundary; decentralized workspaces give finer-grained access, retention, and data-sovereignty control at the cost of harder cross-workspace querying — a regulated subsidiary that needs its own retention period and access boundary is a strong signal for a dedicated workspace even inside an otherwise centralized design. None of this data shows up automatically, though: a diagnostic setting is the specific configuration on a resource that actually routes its platform logs and metrics to a destination, whether that's a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account, or an Event Hub — without one configured, a resource's logs simply aren't being collected anywhere.

Once that telemetry is flowing, Azure Monitor splits it into two different tools suited to two different questions. Metrics are lightweight, numerical time-series data, well suited to fast, near-real-time alerting on something like CPU or memory crossing a threshold. Logs are detailed, structured or free-form records stored in that Log Analytics workspace and queried with KQL, suited to deep, multi-table investigation rather than an instant threshold check. Reaching for Logs when you need a fast, simple alert adds query latency you don't need; reaching for Metrics when you need a complex, correlated investigation doesn't give you the structure to support it. Two more tools round out ongoing governance at this scale: Azure Advisor analyzes what's actually deployed and how it's being used, then generates personalized recommendations organized by those same five Well-Architected pillars, while Azure Resource Graph queries resource metadata across many subscriptions at once with a Kusto-like query language — useful for auditing what's actually out there, even though, unlike Azure Policy, it doesn't enforce or remediate anything itself.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to org-wide governance design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of the management group hierarchy the way a franchise chain sets policy. Corporate sets a handful of non-negotiable rules once, at the top, and every franchise location inherits them automatically without corporate having to visit each location individually — while each location owner still runs their own day-to-day operations underneath that shared umbrella. A landing zone is like corporate handing a brand-new franchisee a fully built-out store, already up to code and already carrying the corporate signage, instead of making them build the whole space from an empty lot themselves.
commonTraps: Only DeployIfNotExists actively fixes existing noncompliant resources — Audit only reports on them, and Deny only blocks new ones from being created.
A landing zone is the deployable environment; the Cloud Adoption Framework is the broader strategy and methodology it implements — they aren't interchangeable terms for the same thing.
Reaching for Logs and KQL for a simple, fast threshold alert adds unnecessary query latency — that's what Metrics and alert rules are for.
A resource's logs aren't collected anywhere by default — a diagnostic setting has to be configured on that resource to actually send them to a destination.
lessons.scenario: An enterprise with a regulated subsidiary is designing its Azure governance from scratch. It creates a management group hierarchy with a top-level group for company-wide policies (mandatory tagging, allowed regions) and deploys new subscriptions through a landing zone so every one starts with that governance, plus hub networking, already in place — following the Cloud Adoption Framework's broader guidance for how to sequence that rollout. Because the subsidiary has its own regulatory retention requirement, its subscription gets a dedicated Log Analytics workspace rather than joining the shared central one, with diagnostic settings configured on its resources to actually route logs there. Company-wide, a fast Metrics-based alert rule pages the on-call engineer within seconds of a VM's CPU spiking, while a deeper, KQL-based Logs query is used the next morning to investigate exactly what caused it — and Azure Advisor's recommendations, along with a Resource Graph query across every subscription, feed into the team's next quarterly review of the whole estate.
lessons.onTheJob: Getting a management group hierarchy and a mandatory tagging policy approved is often less about the technical design and more about which team loses autonomy — a subsidiary that's run its own subscription for years will resist inheriting central policy even when it's clearly the right call. Centralized versus decentralized Log Analytics workspaces is a fight that resurfaces every time a new regulated business unit joins the tenant, and the cheaper answer on paper often loses to a compliance team that won't accept sharing an access boundary. Landing zones sound like a one-time setup cost in a proposal, but in practice they quietly determine how painful every future workload onboarding will be, which is exactly why the upfront investment gets pushback before anyone's felt the payoff.

lessons.title: Data Storage Solutions
lessons.summary: Choosing a SQL hosting model, Cosmos DB consistency and partitioning, storage redundancy and access tiers, and moving data in and out securely.
lessons.reading:
Designing where a relational workload actually lives comes down to how much of the SQL Server engine you need versus how little you want to manage. Azure SQL Database, a single database, is fully managed platform-as-a-service with the least administrative overhead, but it doesn't expose every instance-level SQL Server feature. SQL Managed Instance sits in between: near-complete SQL Server engine compatibility, including SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, and linked servers, while staying fully managed PaaS. SQL Server running on a virtual machine gives full operating system and engine control for maximum compatibility, at the cost of patching and managing that OS yourself. A migration that depends on SQL Agent jobs or cross-database queries, but still wants to avoid managing the OS, points squarely at Managed Instance rather than Azure SQL Database.

For non-relational, globally distributed data, Cosmos DB exposes five consistency levels along a single spectrum, from Strong (no staleness, but the highest latency and lowest availability) down to Eventual (the lowest latency and highest availability, with no ordering guarantee at all) — Session, the default, fits most single-user scenarios where someone needs to see their own writes immediately, while Eventual fits read-heavy, shared workloads that can tolerate a few seconds of staleness for speed. Just as important as consistency is partition key design: a good partition key has high cardinality and spreads requests and storage evenly across physical partitions, while a low-cardinality key concentrates traffic onto a small number of partitions, creating a hot partition that throttles throughput no matter how much RU/s is provisioned. The fix for a hot partition is redesigning the partition key itself — raising the consistency level or adding more provisioned throughput doesn't touch the real problem.

Storage redundancy answers a different question: how many copies of your data exist, and how far apart are they? Locally-redundant storage (LRS) keeps three synchronous copies within one datacenter — the cheapest option, but it only survives a hardware-level failure. Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) spreads those synchronous copies across availability zones within the same region instead, surviving the loss of an entire datacenter without the cost or latency of replicating to a second region. Geo-redundant storage (GRS) asynchronously replicates to a paired secondary region, without any zone redundancy in the primary region itself, while geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) combines both — zone redundancy at home and geo-replication to a second region — for the strongest protection available. Only the read-access ("RA-") variants of GRS or GZRS actually let an application read from that secondary region before a real failover ever happens.

Everyday storage management layers a few more decisions on top. Access tiers trade storage cost against retrieval cost and speed: Hot suits data you touch constantly, at the highest storage cost and cheapest access; Cool and Cold suit infrequently accessed data; and Archive is the cheapest tier of all, but blobs have to be rehydrated, a process that can take hours, before they can be read again — the right pick when cost matters more than instant access, never when data needs to be readable at a moment's notice. For large-scale analytics, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob storage with a hierarchical namespace turned on, giving engines like Synapse or Databricks POSIX-like access control and efficient directory-level operations instead of flat object storage. When it's time to actually migrate a database, Data Migration Assistant assesses an on-premises database for compatibility issues before anything moves, while Database Migration Service performs the real migration, online or offline, once you're ready — DMA answers "will this break after we move it," DMS is the tool that actually moves it. And for reaching a PaaS data service privately, a private endpoint gives it a private IP address inside your VNet, reachable even from on-premises networks over ExpressRoute or a VPN, while a service endpoint keeps the public IP in place and only optimizes and restricts routing for traffic that already starts inside the VNet — only a private endpoint reaches a PaaS service privately from on-premises.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Azure data platform trade-offs? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing between Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, and SQL Server on a VM is like choosing an apartment, a townhouse, or a standalone house: the apartment (Azure SQL Database) has the least upkeep but the least customization; the townhouse (Managed Instance) gives you more of your own space and rules while someone else still handles the roof and the plumbing; the house (a VM) gives total control, but you're the one calling a repair person, or being one, for every single thing that breaks. Storage redundancy is like deciding how many copies of your family photos to keep, and how far apart: one copy in a drawer (LRS) protects against a spill, copies split across two rooms of the same house (ZRS) protect against a room flooding, and a copy at a relative's house in another city (GRS/GZRS) is the only thing that survives the whole house burning down.
commonTraps: A hot partition is fixed by redesigning the partition key itself — raising the consistency level or adding more RU/s doesn't solve an uneven partition key.
Archive tier is the cheapest to store, but blobs need rehydration, which can take hours, before they're readable again — don't pick it for data that must be available instantly.
Plain GRS replicates to a secondary region, but that copy isn't readable until an actual failover — only the read-access (RA-) variants can be read from directly beforehand.
A service endpoint only optimizes traffic that already starts inside the VNet — reaching a PaaS resource privately from on-premises specifically requires a private endpoint.
lessons.scenario: A healthcare analytics company is migrating an on-premises SQL Server database that relies on SQL Agent jobs and needs its Data Lake Storage Gen2 account reachable privately from its on-premises network over ExpressRoute. It runs Data Migration Assistant first to catch compatibility issues, then targets SQL Managed Instance rather than Azure SQL Database, since Managed Instance supports SQL Agent jobs while still avoiding OS management, and uses Database Migration Service for the actual online migration. For its Cosmos DB telemetry store, it redesigns a low-cardinality partition key that was creating a hot partition, and keeps Session consistency since each device needs to see its own latest writes immediately. Its storage account is configured for GZRS, protecting both against a single datacenter's loss and a full regional outage, with a lifecycle policy moving telemetry older than a year into Archive tier, and a private endpoint — not a service endpoint — providing the required private, on-premises reachability.
lessons.onTheJob: Choosing Managed Instance over Azure SQL Database because of SQL Agent jobs is a decision an architect often has to defend twice — once to a DBA team attached to its legacy tooling, and again to a finance stakeholder who sees the bigger line item and assumes it's over-engineering. GZRS and an Archive-tier lifecycle policy look great in a cost-optimization slide until a client remembers that rehydrating archived data takes hours, at which point the real conversation becomes what data can actually tolerate that delay versus what the business insists it can't. Partition key redesign for Cosmos DB is the kind of fix that's cheap on a whiteboard and genuinely painful in production, since it usually means a data migration the client didn't budget for when they signed off on the original design. A Data Migration Assistant report that comes back clean is also not the same thing as a guaranteed-compatible migration — CLR assemblies, specific SQL Agent proxy accounts, and other instance-level quirks DMA doesn't fully evaluate are exactly why a real proof-of-concept restore into a non-production Managed Instance is worth doing even after a spotless assessment.

lessons.title: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
lessons.summary: RTO/RPO-driven design, Azure Backup vs. Azure Site Recovery, availability zones vs. paired regions, and active-active vs. active-passive.
lessons.reading:
Every business continuity design should start from two numbers the business sets, not the other way around: RTO (recovery time objective), the maximum tolerable downtime, and RPO (recovery point objective), the maximum tolerable data loss. Only once those numbers are known does it make sense to pick a backup frequency, a replication approach, and how much failover automation to build — a design question that states specific RTO/RPO numbers is really asking for the cheapest architecture that still satisfies both, not the most impressive-sounding one available.

Two Azure services get confused constantly because they sound similar but protect against entirely different things. Azure Backup protects data: it restores a file, a VM, or a database to an earlier point in time, which is exactly what you want after accidental deletion or corruption. Azure Site Recovery protects availability instead, replicating an entire VM or workload to a secondary region or zone so it can fail over and keep running through an outage. A request to recover an accidentally deleted file points to Backup; a request to keep an application running after a whole region goes down points to Site Recovery. Both actually live inside the same Recovery Services vault, which stores backup data as well as Site Recovery's replication configuration and metadata — and it's easy to assume backups automatically survive a regional outage, when that actually depends entirely on the vault's own redundancy setting (LRS, GRS, or zone-redundant), which is worth checking explicitly rather than assuming.

Two different failure scopes call for two different tools working together, not one replacing the other. Availability zones give synchronous, low-latency redundancy across physically separate datacenters within a single region, protecting against the loss of one datacenter. A secondary region — paired with the primary — provides asynchronous disaster-recovery redundancy against a full regional disaster instead, at the cost of higher replication latency — a well-designed solution frequently uses both together rather than choosing one over the other. How a multi-region design actually behaves during a failure comes down to active-active versus active-passive: active-active runs full production traffic in two or more regions at once, giving the fastest possible recovery at the highest cost and complexity, including handling conflicting writes made in two places at once; active-passive keeps a warm or cold standby region that only takes over after a failover, cheaper but slower to recover. "Zero perceptible downtime during a regional failure" is the signal phrase for active-active; any standby that has to be activated first, warm or cold, is active-passive.

Some Azure services build failover automation in directly. Azure SQL Database auto-failover groups replicate one or more databases on a logical server to a secondary region and expose stable read-write and read-only listener endpoints that automatically redirect after a failover — so an application's connection string never has to change. That same read-only listener can actually serve reads from the secondary region even before any failover occurs, not only afterward, which is a detail worth remembering since it's easy to assume the secondary sits completely idle until disaster strikes.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to business continuity design? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Backup is like keeping dated copies of an important document, so you can go back to yesterday's version if today's got corrupted or deleted — it fixes a data problem. Site Recovery is like having a fully-equipped second office ready to open immediately if your main building becomes unusable — not just a copy of your files, but an entire working replacement environment standing by, ready to actually run the business. Active-active is like already having both offices open and staffed every single day, so losing one changes nothing for customers; active-passive is like keeping the second office's lights off and unstaffed until the day you actually need to open its doors.
commonTraps: Backup restores a point-in-time copy of data; Site Recovery fails over an entire running workload to another region — they solve different problems and often coexist in the same design.
A Recovery Services vault's own storage redundancy setting determines whether backups survive a regional outage — don't assume they automatically do just because the vault exists.
"Zero perceptible downtime" during a regional failure describes active-active, not active-passive — any standby that must be activated first, warm or cold, is active-passive.
The read-only listener of an auto-failover group can already serve reads from the secondary region before any failover happens — the secondary isn't sitting completely idle.
lessons.scenario: A payments company sets its RTO at under two minutes and its RPO at near-zero for its core transaction database, and is willing to pay for the infrastructure that meets those numbers. It deploys Azure SQL Database with auto-failover groups across two regions in an active-active-leaning design, so the application's connection string never has to change during a failover, and configures its VM tier with availability zones for datacenter-level resilience plus Azure Site Recovery for full regional failover. Its nightly backups go to a Recovery Services vault explicitly configured for geo-redundant storage, since the original LRS default vault setting would have meant those backups couldn't survive the very regional outage the design is meant to withstand.
lessons.onTheJob: RTO and RPO numbers a client states in a workshop are often aspirational rather than actually costed out, so a real part of the job is translating 'we need near-zero downtime' into the dollar figure active-active multi-region actually costs, and watching how fast that appetite changes once the client sees it. Backup and Site Recovery get bundled into one line item in budget conversations even though they solve different problems, and the closest calls to a real incident are almost always the ones where a team assumed backups already survived a regional outage without ever checking the vault's own redundancy setting. Active-passive gets sold as basically the same as active-active for a fraction of the cost, which is true right up until an actual regional failure, when the failover time nobody stress-tested becomes the client's first real data point. Auto-failover groups also get quietly undermined by a shortcut: a developer who hardcodes the primary server's own connection string instead of the read-write listener endpoint will see everything work fine for months, right up until a real failover happens and that hardcoded string stops resolving to anything live.

lessons.title: Compute & Networking Architecture
lessons.summary: Choosing a compute service, hub-and-spoke topology, connecting networks together, distributing traffic, and filtering it.
lessons.reading:
Choosing compute for a new architecture is really a question of how much control you need against how much operational burden you're willing to take on. A virtual machine gives full operating system control, suited to legacy or highly specialized workloads that need it. App Service is managed platform-as-a-service web hosting with no orchestration layer to manage at all. AKS gives full Kubernetes control for complex microservices that genuinely need custom orchestration. Container Apps runs serverless containers with built-in, HTTP or event-based autoscaling and common microservices patterns, without you ever managing a cluster. And Functions is event-driven, per-execution billed compute, ideal for short-lived triggered code. "Wants container-based autoscaling but doesn't want to manage a cluster" is the classic signal pointing to Container Apps over AKS.

For networking at scale, a hub-and-spoke topology puts shared services — a firewall, a VPN or ExpressRoute gateway, DNS — into a central hub VNet, while spoke VNets, one per workload or team, peer only to the hub and not to each other. That isolation is frequently the whole point of the design: by default, peering to a shared hub does not let two spokes talk to each other directly, and an Azure landing zone typically ships this topology already built for new workloads to land into. Connecting VNets and networks to each other has three main options, each solving a different problem. VNet peering connects Azure VNets directly over Microsoft's own backbone, with low latency and no gateway required. A Site-to-Site VPN Gateway connects an on-premises network to Azure over an encrypted tunnel across the public internet — cheaper and faster to stand up, but subject to internet variability. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit to Azure through a connectivity provider, bypassing the public internet entirely for the highest, most predictable bandwidth and latency, which is the answer whenever a scenario specifically calls for that predictability.

Distributing traffic across an architecture calls for a different service depending on scope and layer. Azure Front Door is a global, layer-7 entry point with edge caching and a Web Application Firewall, routing across regions. Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer, offering its own Web Application Firewall but only within one region. Traffic Manager is purely DNS-based global routing with no data-plane inspection at all — it only returns which endpoint's IP address a client should use next, so its failover is limited by client-side DNS caching (TTL), unlike Front Door's real data-plane failover. Filtering that traffic at the network layer has its own two-tier choice: a network security group (NSG) is a simple, free, per-subnet or per-NIC allow/deny filter on IP address, port, and protocol, while Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, centralized firewall that also supports FQDN-based filtering and unified logging across many VNets — since NSGs have no concept of a fully qualified domain name, FQDN-based outbound filtering across a whole hub-and-spoke estate calls for Azure Firewall, not a pile of per-subnet NSGs.

Two more decisions round out this design space. Scaling an App Service plan up changes its pricing tier or size to a bigger instance; scaling out adds more instances of that same tier, often automated through autoscale rules based on metrics or a schedule — autoscale rules configure scaling out, never a tier change. And regardless of what gets built, Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — declarative ARM, Bicep, or Terraform templates that get version-controlled, reviewed, and deployed repeatably — is how a design requiring consistent, repeatable, auditable deployments across multiple environments actually gets delivered, instead of manually clicking through the portal each time.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Azure compute and networking trade-offs? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Choosing a compute option is like choosing how much of a meal to cook yourself: a VM is buying raw ingredients and cooking entirely from scratch, App Service is a meal kit where the basics are already handled, and Functions is ordering delivery — you specify what you want and it just appears, with none of the kitchen work on your end. A hub-and-spoke network is like an office building with a shared reception desk and security team in the lobby (the hub), while each floor (a spoke) runs its own business independently — floors don't get to walk straight into each other, they all funnel back through that shared lobby first.
commonTraps: Container Apps adds built-in autoscaling without you managing a cluster — AKS is the one that hands you full cluster control (and full cluster responsibility).
VNet peering isn't transitive: peering A to B and B to C doesn't let A and C talk to each other without their own direct peering.
Traffic Manager only makes DNS-layer decisions — it never inspects or proxies the actual HTTP traffic the way Front Door or Application Gateway do.
NSGs have no concept of an FQDN — centralized, FQDN-based outbound filtering across a hub-and-spoke estate needs Azure Firewall, not more NSG rules.
lessons.scenario: A retailer is redesigning its Azure networking and compute footprint. It builds a hub-and-spoke topology, with Azure Firewall in the hub doing FQDN-based outbound filtering that individual NSGs in each spoke can't provide, and an ExpressRoute circuit connecting the hub back to its on-premises datacenter for predictable, high-bandwidth traffic. Its new checkout microservices go into Container Apps, since the team wants built-in autoscaling under Black Friday traffic without taking on cluster management, while a legacy inventory system that needs full OS access stays on a VM. Globally, Azure Front Door sits in front of the whole storefront, caching static assets at the edge and enforcing a Web Application Firewall across every region — deliberately not Traffic Manager, since the retailer specifically needs real content-aware routing and failover, not just a DNS answer. Every piece of this — the hub, the spokes, the firewall rules, the Front Door configuration — is deployed through Bicep templates checked into source control, so the whole environment can be rebuilt consistently in a new region if it ever needs to be.
lessons.onTheJob: Container Apps versus AKS is as much an organizational-maturity question as a technical one — a team pushing for AKS because it's what they already know is a common design-review fight, and the architect's real job is separating 'we genuinely need custom orchestration' from 'we don't want to learn something new.' ExpressRoute gets proposed constantly for its predictable latency, right up until procurement sees the monthly cost and asks whether a Site-to-Site VPN would really be that much worse — a question that usually has a real, testable answer instead of a gut-feel one. Azure Firewall's FQDN filtering sounds like nice-to-have governance in a proposal, but it becomes the thing everyone's grateful for the day someone has to reconstruct what an entire hub-and-spoke estate's outbound traffic rules actually allow. The Infrastructure as Code (IaC) discipline that closes out this design — version-controlled Bicep or Terraform instead of manual portal clicks — is the same concept CompTIA's Cloud+ exam tests vendor-neutrally, and it's the reason a hub-and-spoke estate built this way can actually be torn down and rebuilt in a new region on demand, rather than existing only as institutional memory of what someone once clicked.

lessons.title: Migration, Messaging & Integration
lessons.summary: Discovering and assessing workloads before a move, choosing the right messaging service, exposing and orchestrating APIs, and troubleshooting the network afterward.
lessons.reading:
Before any large migration begins, Azure Migrate serves as the hub for discovery and assessment — finding on-premises servers and workloads, right-sizing them, checking readiness, and estimating cost, all before a single workload actually moves. The real data migration itself is often handed off afterward to a more specialized tool, like Database Migration Service for a database, once Azure Migrate's assessment says a workload is actually ready to go.

Once workloads are in Azure, connecting them together calls for the right messaging or eventing service, and these three get mixed up constantly. Service Bus is a message broker built for ordered, transactional, point-to-point or publish/subscribe messaging with guaranteed delivery — the right choice when an order has to be processed exactly once, in order. Event Grid is a lightweight, reactive eventing service for discrete event notifications with push-based routing, suited to reacting to something like "a blob was created" rather than processing a queue of work. Event Hubs is built for high-throughput streaming and telemetry ingestion at a massive scale, the pick when the requirement is high-volume data ingestion rather than reliable, ordered processing.

Exposing and orchestrating that backend often needs its own layer, too. Azure API Management is a facade placed in front of backend APIs regardless of how or where they're actually hosted — VMs, App Service, anything — adding one consistent gateway for authentication, rate limiting, versioning, and a developer portal, so API consumers are decoupled from the underlying implementation. For integration logic itself, Logic Apps is a low-code, designer-driven workflow orchestrator with hundreds of prebuilt connectors, well suited to integrating SaaS and enterprise systems in a way business analysts, not just developers, can follow and adjust. Azure Functions is code-first, event-triggered compute instead, better suited when custom logic or fine-grained execution control is the real priority.

At the largest scale, Azure Virtual WAN automates hub-and-spoke connectivity — branch offices, VPN and ExpressRoute connections, hubs, and routing — across many regions at once, instead of hand-building and peering each regional hub yourself. Day to day, once a network is actually built, Network Watcher provides the diagnostic tools to troubleshoot it: IP flow verify checks whether a specific rule is allowing or blocking a given flow, NSG flow logs record every flow that gets evaluated, and Connection Troubleshoot runs an end-to-end reachability test — these are diagnostics for a network that already exists, not design-time governance controls. And for secure administrative access into that network, Azure Bastion provides RDP or SSH through the portal itself, without ever exposing a VM's public IP address — a detail worth remembering whenever a scenario asks for remote access without any public IP exposure at all.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to Azure integration and eventing? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Service Bus, Event Grid, and Event Hubs are like three different ways a business handles incoming information. Service Bus is like a certified mail queue — every item gets processed, in order, exactly once, with a signature confirming delivery. Event Grid is like a text alert telling a manager the instant something specific happens, with no ongoing queue to process. Event Hubs is like a firehose of sensor readings pouring in continuously — the goal isn't to process each drop individually, it's to capture and analyze the whole stream at massive volume.
commonTraps: Azure Migrate is for discovery and assessment before a move — the actual migration is usually carried out by a more specialized tool like Database Migration Service.

Event Grid reacts to discrete events like a resource being created; Service Bus is for reliable, ordered message processing; Event Hubs is for high-throughput streaming ingestion — picking the wrong one for the requirement is the most common trap here.
Logic Apps and Azure Functions both do integration work, but a requirement that non-developers understand and adjust the flow points to Logic Apps, not hand-written Functions code.
Network Watcher's tools troubleshoot a network that's already built — they don't govern or restrict how it gets built in the first place.
lessons.scenario: A logistics company is migrating a fleet of on-premises servers and building new cloud-native integration around them. It starts with Azure Migrate to discover and assess every server before touching anything, then hands the actual database move to Database Migration Service once the assessment clears. Its new order-processing pipeline uses Service Bus, since each order must be processed exactly once and in order, while a separate "a new shipment label was generated" notification fans out through Event Grid to several independent subscribers. External partners access the company's shipping API through Azure API Management, which enforces a consistent authentication and rate-limiting layer regardless of which backend actually serves each call, while a Logic Apps workflow — built and maintained by the operations team, not developers — handles the day-to-day integration between the SaaS CRM and the on-premises ERP system. When a connectivity issue is reported, Network Watcher's IP flow verify quickly confirms which rule in the hub-and-spoke network is actually blocking the traffic.
lessons.onTheJob: A migration assessment from Azure Migrate almost never comes back as clean as the client hoped, and a real part of the job is having the 'your legacy dependency on SQL Agent jobs isn't going away just because we moved to the cloud' conversation before it becomes a surprise mid-migration. Picking Service Bus over Event Grid or Event Hubs looks like a pure technical decision until a team used to fire-and-forget messaging has to actually learn ordered, transactional processing, and the pushback there is really about operational comfort, not correctness. Logic Apps gets pitched because business analysts can maintain it without a developer, but the unglamorous reality is that whoever built the original workflow usually ends up as the only person who actually understands its edge cases, no-code promise notwithstanding.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: You have 120 minutes for 50 questions — about 2.4 minutes each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.
Real scoring isn't a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — treat 75%+ as a safe buffer to aim for, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and you get partial credit for nothing by running out of time on one question.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: Well-Architected Framework pillars
points: The five pillars are Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency — every design decision on this exam should trace back to a tradeoff among these.
Reliability = a workload keeps running and recovers from failure; it directly drives RTO/RPO decisions, redundancy, and DR design.
Cost Optimization doesn't mean cheapest — it means the right spend for the value delivered, which is why "most cost-effective" answers still have to meet the stated requirements.
Performance Efficiency is about a workload scaling to meet demand efficiently, not just raw speed — think autoscaling and right-sizing, not just "the fastest SKU."

cheatSheet.heading: Identity & governance architecture
points: Hierarchy is Management Groups → Subscriptions → Resource Groups → Resources; Azure Policy and RBAC assignments both inherit downward through this hierarchy.

Azure Policy enforces compliance on resource CONFIGURATION (effects like Deny, Audit, Append, Modify, DeployIfNotExists); RBAC controls WHO can perform WHICH actions — a design needs both, not one instead of the other.

Landing zones (per the Cloud Adoption Framework) separate platform landing zones (shared identity, connectivity, management) from application landing zones (workload-specific resources) — design shared services once, reuse across workloads.
Prefer management-group-level policy assignments over repeating the same policy in every subscription when a rule must apply organization-wide.

cheatSheet.heading: Compute design tradeoffs
points: Control vs. management overhead spectrum: VMs/VMSS (most control, most overhead) → AKS (full orchestration control, real ops burden) → Container Apps (serverless containers, less to manage) → App Service (PaaS web apps, least infrastructure to manage) → Functions (event-driven serverless, pay-per-execution).

Choose AKS when you need deep Kubernetes-level control (custom schedulers, service mesh, multi-container pods); choose Container Apps or App Service when you just need to run containers/web apps without managing a cluster.
Azure Functions Consumption plan scales to zero and bills per execution; Premium/Dedicated plans trade some of that elasticity for pre-warmed instances and VNet integration.

cheatSheet.heading: Storage design tradeoffs
points: Redundancy choice should be driven by required durability and DR scope: LRS/ZRS protect within a region (datacenter vs. zone failure); GRS/RA-GRS/GZRS/RA-GZRS add protection against a full regional outage, with the RA- variants also allowing reads from the secondary.

Blob access tiers (Hot/Cool/Cold/Archive) are a cost-vs-access-latency design lever, not just an operational setting — Archive needs rehydration before it can be read, so it's wrong for anything needing fast recovery.
Premium SSD or Ultra Disk for latency-sensitive, high-IOPS workloads (databases); Standard tiers for dev/test or infrequently accessed data.

cheatSheet.heading: Networking design tradeoffs
points: Hub-and-spoke topology centralizes shared services (firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute gateway, DNS) in a hub VNet, with workload VNets as spokes peered to it — spokes don't automatically talk to each other through the hub without explicit routing (peering is non-transitive).
Azure Virtual WAN automates hub-and-spoke connectivity at large/global scale, replacing manually-managed hubs when you have many regions/sites.

Front Door = global Layer 7 load balancing with WAF + CDN (best for global-scale web apps). Traffic Manager = global DNS-based routing, protocol-agnostic (works for non-HTTP too). Application Gateway = regional Layer 7 with WAF. Load Balancer = regional/zonal Layer 4 — pick based on required scope AND protocol, not just "global vs. regional."

cheatSheet.heading: Business continuity & DR design
points: Always define RTO (max acceptable downtime) and RPO (max acceptable data loss) FIRST from business requirements — they determine which redundancy/DR service is actually correct, not the other way around.
Availability Zones protect against a datacenter-level failure within one region; only a multi-region design protects against a full regional outage.

Azure Backup handles point-in-time data recovery; Azure Site Recovery handles full workload/region failover — a DR design combining both often needs Backup for granular recovery and Site Recovery for the region-level failover story.

Paired regions get sequential platform update rollout and are the default target for geo-redundant storage replication — factor that into region-pair selection for compliance/data-residency requirements too.

cheatSheet.heading: Migration strategy basics
points: The migration strategies (the "R's"): Rehost (lift-and-shift, fastest, least change), Refactor/Re-platform (small optimizations, e.g. move to a managed database), Rearchitect (redesign for cloud-native scale), Rebuild (start over cloud-native), Retire (decommission what's no longer needed).
Azure Migrate is the central hub for discovery, assessment, and migration of servers, databases, and web apps at scale — start there before picking point tools.
Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) performs the actual database migration (offline or online/minimal-downtime); Data Migration Assistant only assesses compatibility beforehand.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day reminders
points: AZ-305 is a design exam — there is often more than one technically valid answer; pick the one that best satisfies ALL stated requirements (cost, compliance, RTO/RPO), not just the most impressive-sounding service.
Case-study-style questions expect you to reference stated constraints (budget, existing on-prem AD, compliance region) rather than a generic best practice that ignores them.
When a requirement says "minimize operational overhead," that pulls toward PaaS/serverless options over IaaS, unless another hard requirement rules that out.

madlibs.scenario: A company wants administrators to hold no standing access to sensitive roles, requesting time-bound elevation with justification only when needed — this calls for {b1}. Separately, they want an easy way to sign in during an emergency if Conditional Access or MFA is ever accidentally misconfigured and locks everyone else out — for that, they set up {b2}, deliberately excluded from the normal sign-in policies.

options: Privileged Identity Management (PIM)
Entitlement management
Access reviews
Azure Policy
a break-glass emergency access account
a second Global Administrator for every team
a Conditional Access exclusion for all users
a service principal with Owner at the tenant root

madlibs.explanation: PIM converts standing privileged access into time-bound, justified activations. A break-glass account is a small number of cloud-only accounts, deliberately excluded from Conditional Access and closely monitored, kept specifically so a misconfigured policy can never lock every administrator out at once — granting broad access to more accounts or excluding everyone would defeat the point of a narrow emergency path.

madlibs.scenario: A storage account needs to survive the loss of an entire datacenter within its region — protected by {b1} — and separately needs its data to also be readable from a second region without waiting for a failover, which additionally requires {b2}.

options: zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
locally-redundant storage (LRS)
a lifecycle management policy
soft delete
read access enabled on a geo-redundant option (RA-GRS or RA-GZRS)
a second storage account manually synced by a script
a private endpoint in the secondary region
Archive tier in the primary region

madlibs.explanation: ZRS synchronously spreads copies across zones in one region, surviving a single datacenter loss. LRS only protects against a hardware failure within one datacenter, not a zone loss. Reading from a secondary region before any failover specifically requires the read-access ('RA-') variant of a geo-redundant option — plain GRS replicates there but keeps that copy unreadable until an actual failover occurs.

madlibs.scenario: A team wants to run containerized microservices with built-in autoscaling on HTTP and event triggers, but explicitly doesn't want to manage cluster upgrades or node pools — that points to {b1}. A different team needs deep control over the Kubernetes API itself, including custom operators, and is willing to manage the cluster to get it — that points to {b2} instead.

options: Azure Container Apps
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure Virtual Machines
Azure Functions on a Premium plan
Azure Container Apps
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure Batch
Azure App Service

madlibs.explanation: Container Apps gives serverless containers with built-in autoscaling and no cluster to manage, matching a team that wants orchestration benefits without the operational burden. AKS gives full Kubernetes API control, including custom operators and schedulers, at the cost of managing the cluster yourself — the right trade for a team that specifically needs that depth of control.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for designing a landing zone that keeps a new workload network-isolated from other workloads.
steps: Create the hub VNet with shared services (firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute gateway)
Create a dedicated spoke VNet for the new workload
Peer the spoke VNet to the hub (not to other spokes)
Apply NSGs and route tables to enforce the isolation boundary
sequences.explanation: The topology decision comes first since it shapes everything after it; the hub has to exist before a spoke can peer to it, and peering spoke-to-hub only (never spoke-to-spoke) is exactly what keeps workloads isolated from each other by default.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for implementing a disaster recovery strategy for a business-critical app with strict RTO/RPO requirements.
steps: Define the required RTO and RPO with the business
Choose a DR pattern that meets those targets (e.g. active-passive with Azure Site Recovery)
Replicate the workload to the secondary region
Test failover regularly without impacting production
Document and rehearse the actual failover/failback runbook
sequences.explanation: You can't choose a DR pattern until you know the actual RTO/RPO targets it needs to hit — designing the technical solution before agreeing the requirement is a common real-world (and exam) trap. Regular testing and a written runbook come last since they validate the solution already built.

sequences.prompt: Put these steps in order for migrating an on-premises SQL Server database to Azure with minimal downtime.
steps: Assess the source database using Data Migration Assistant
Choose the migration target (Azure SQL Database, Managed Instance, or SQL on a VM)
Set up Azure Database Migration Service
Perform an initial full data migration
Enable continuous sync to keep the target updated
Cut over during a scheduled maintenance window and redirect the application
sequences.explanation: Assessment has to happen before you can commit to a target (some compatibility issues rule out certain targets entirely). Continuous sync after the initial migration is what actually enables a low-downtime cutover — without it, cutover would require a long final full copy while the app is offline.

caseStudies.title: Contoso Retail's Global Storefront Migration
caseStudies.scenario: Contoso Retail runs its e-commerce storefront from a single datacenter in Chicago. The storefront is a containerized .NET application that the team already packages as Docker images, and traffic is heavily seasonal — Black Friday weekend sees 20x normal load, while most of the year the app runs well below capacity. The database tier is a SQL Server instance holding the product catalog and order history; the business requires it to remain available even if an entire Azure region goes offline. Contoso's platform team is small and does not want to manage Kubernetes control planes or patch VM operating systems by hand. Customers are located across North America, Europe, and Asia, and Contoso wants a single application endpoint that automatically routes each customer to their nearest healthy deployment.

questions.question: Given the platform team's size and its wish to avoid managing Kubernetes control planes or patching VM operating systems, which compute service should be recommended for the containerized storefront?
options: Azure Container Apps
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Azure Virtual Machines running Docker
Azure Kubernetes Service with the cluster autoscaler
questions.explanation: Azure Container Apps runs containers on a fully-managed Kubernetes-based platform without exposing (or requiring anyone to manage) the control plane, VM patching, or node pools — a direct fit for a small team that explicitly wants none of that operational burden. AKS (with or without the cluster autoscaler) still hands the team a control plane and node pool to operate, and running Docker directly on VMs reintroduces the OS-patching work the scenario says to avoid.

questions.question: Which scaling approach best fits the storefront's 20x seasonal traffic swing between Black Friday and the rest of the year?
options: Provision fixed capacity sized for Black Friday peak year-round
Scale automatically based on HTTP traffic and CPU/memory metrics, scaling to zero when idle
Manually resize the deployment before and after each expected peak
Provision fixed capacity sized for average traffic and accept slower response times during peaks
questions.explanation: Automatic, metrics-driven scaling (including scale-to-zero) matches spend to actual demand, handling the 20x Black Friday spike without paying for that much capacity the other 51 weeks of the year. Fixed capacity at either peak or average levels wastes money most of the year or fails during peak; manual resizing depends on someone correctly predicting exact peak timing, which is exactly the operational burden autoscaling removes.

questions.question: Which storage redundancy option should be recommended for the SQL Server database given the requirement that it survive an entire regional outage?
options: Locally-redundant storage (LRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) or geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Read-access geo-redundant storage is unnecessary if backups run nightly
questions.explanation: Only GRS/GZRS replicate data to a secondary Azure region, which is what surviving a full regional outage requires. LRS and ZRS both replicate only within the primary region (ZRS across availability zones, but still one region), so neither protects against that region going offline entirely. Nightly backups alone would still mean a real recovery-time gap and don't by themselves place a copy of the data in another region.
questions.whyTested: AZ-305 case studies frequently bury the real requirement ("survive a regional outage") inside a paragraph of unrelated detail — recognizing that single sentence as the one that rules out every region-local redundancy option is the actual skill being tested, not memorizing the redundancy tiers in isolation.

questions.question: Which Azure service should route each customer to their nearest healthy regional deployment through a single application endpoint?
options: Azure Front Door
Azure Load Balancer
A single Application Gateway shared across all regions
Azure Traffic Manager only, with no Front Door or Application Gateway
questions.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global, HTTP(S)-aware entry point that performs latency-based routing to the nearest healthy backend region behind one endpoint, plus health probes and failover — exactly what a global storefront with regional deployments needs. Azure Load Balancer operates within a single region, not across them. A single Application Gateway is also regional. Traffic Manager alone works at the DNS layer and lacks Front Door's Layer-7 features (like path-based routing and web application firewall integration), making Front Door the better fit for an HTTP storefront specifically.

caseStudies.title: Fabrikam Insurance's Claims Processing Recovery Plan
caseStudies.scenario: Fabrikam Insurance runs a claims-processing application on Azure SQL Database in a single primary region. The business has set a strict recovery point objective (RPO) of under 5 seconds and a recovery time objective (RTO) of under 1 minute for the claims database, since adjusters must never lose an in-progress claim and downtime directly delays payouts. Separately, the company's internal claims-review web app runs on a handful of Azure Virtual Machines; for that workload, the business can tolerate up to 4 hours of downtime and up to 15 minutes of data loss if the primary region fails, and wants failover to be triggered automatically rather than requiring someone to be paged in the middle of the night. Fabrikam's compliance team also requires that every failover test be rehearsed without ever impacting the live production environment.

questions.question: Which Azure SQL Database feature should be recommended to meet the claims database's sub-5-second RPO and sub-1-minute RTO?
options: Auto-failover groups with active geo-replication
A nightly automated backup with point-in-time restore
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) on the underlying storage account
A manually-triggered geo-restore from backup
questions.explanation: Auto-failover groups keep a continuously synchronized secondary replica and can fail over automatically within roughly a minute, meeting both the aggressive RPO and RTO. Nightly backups and geo-restore both imply recovery measured in potentially hours with data loss back to the last backup, not seconds. GRS protects the storage layer, not a live, queryable database replica, and doesn't by itself deliver an application-consistent database failover.

questions.question: True or false: for the claims-review VMs, whose business tolerance is up to 4 hours RTO and 15 minutes RPO with automatic failover, Azure Site Recovery replicating to a secondary region is an appropriate solution.
questions.explanation: Azure Site Recovery is built for exactly this profile — VM-level replication to a secondary region with typical RPOs in the minutes and orchestrated (including automatic) failover, comfortably meeting a 4-hour RTO/15-minute RPO target without requiring the much tighter (and costlier) synchronous replication a sub-minute RTO would demand.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about meeting the compliance team's requirement to rehearse failover without impacting production? (Select all that apply.)
options: Azure Site Recovery supports test failover into an isolated network, leaving the production VMs and replication untouched
A test failover validates the replicated copy is recoverable without triggering an actual failover of production traffic
The only way to validate DR readiness is to perform a real failover of production traffic on a schedule
Test failover should be run against an isolated virtual network, not the production VNet, to avoid IP or naming conflicts
questions.explanation: Azure Site Recovery's test failover feature spins up recovered VMs in an isolated network specifically so the drill validates recoverability without ever touching live production traffic or replication — which is why it should target an isolated VNet rather than production's, avoiding IP/naming collisions with the still-running primary. Requiring a real production failover on a schedule is the opposite of what the compliance requirement ("never impacting live production") asks for, and isn't how Site Recovery test failovers are meant to be exercised.

compare.scenario: A company is lifting a legacy line-of-business app to Azure. The app needs LDAP, Kerberos, and NTLM authentication, but no schema extensions or custom domain-controller configuration, and the team wants as little domain-controller administration as possible. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Windows Server AD DS domain controllers on Azure VMs, added to the on-premises forest as a new site.
compare.optionB: Microsoft Entra Domain Services, a managed domain whose domain controllers Microsoft patches and monitors.
compare.why: Entra Domain Services supplies LDAP, Kerberos, and NTLM from managed domain controllers, so nobody patches, backs up, or monitors them, which fits an app with no schema-extension needs. AD DS on VMs would work and is the right call when you need schema extensions, full domain admin rights, or forest trusts, but this team would own OS patching, replication health, and backups for every controller with no requirement that justifies it.

compare.scenario: A weekly-rebuilt test environment has a VM that reads one secret from Key Vault each night. Security wants the VM's identity deleted automatically whenever the VM is deleted, so no unused identity is left behind. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: A system-assigned managed identity on the VM, with the Key Vault role granted to that identity.
compare.optionB: A user-assigned managed identity created once and attached to each rebuilt VM, granted the role once.
compare.why: A system-assigned identity shares the VM's lifecycle: it is created with the VM and deleted with it, so nothing is left behind. A user-assigned identity is the better tool when several resources share one identity or the identity must outlive any one resource, and reusing it across rebuilds would save role-assignment work, but it is a standalone resource that stays in the tenant after the VM is gone, which is exactly what security wants to avoid.

compare.scenario: A tenant has about 1,800 guest users who were invited directly into Microsoft 365 groups over three years. Nobody remembers who still needs access, and access packages were never used. The company wants group owners to confirm periodically who should keep access. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Entitlement management access packages with an expiration, to which the guests must re-request access.
compare.optionB: A recurring access review of the guest members of those groups, removing guests that are not confirmed.
compare.why: Access reviews are built to recertify access that already exists: group owners confirm or remove each guest, and unconfirmed guests can be removed automatically. Entitlement management gives time-boxed access going forward, but these guests were never granted access through packages, so using it would mean building packages and asking all 1,800 guests to re-request access, far more work for the same outcome.

compare.scenario: A game company stores player profiles as key-value entities. Players on three continents need single-digit-millisecond reads, writes accepted in the nearest region, and automatic regional failover without an administrator stepping in. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, with multi-region writes enabled in the three player regions.
compare.optionB: Azure Table storage in an RA-GZRS account, read from the secondary endpoint by distant players.
compare.why: Cosmos DB replicates to the chosen regions with low-latency reads, and with multi-region writes each player writes to the nearest region and survives a regional loss without a manual step. Table storage is cheaper and fits simple key-value data, but even with RA-GZRS it has a single write region and a read-only secondary, so distant players write across continents, and recovering from a regional outage needs an administrator-triggered account failover.

compare.scenario: An internal reporting app uses an Azure SQL database that is queried heavily for about three hours on weekdays and sits idle overnight and on weekends. Load varies from day to day, and the team wants to pay for compute only while it is in use. Which is the better choice?
compare.optionA: A provisioned General Purpose database sized for the daily peak, scaled down at night by a scheduled script.
compare.optionB: A serverless General Purpose database with auto-pause and a configured minimum and maximum vCore range.
compare.why: Serverless scales compute within the configured vCore range as load changes and auto-pauses when idle, billing only for storage while paused, which suits an unpredictable three-hour daily window. Scripting a scale-down on a provisioned database also cuts cost, but compute is still billed around the clock at the lower size, resizing briefly drops connections, and the team has to build and maintain the script and its schedule.

compare.scenario: An HTTPS storefront runs in two regions. The business wants users moved away from a failed region within about 30 seconds, but browsers and corporate resolvers cache DNS answers. Which is the better routing layer?
compare.optionA: Azure Front Door, with health probes against both regional origins.
compare.optionB: Azure Traffic Manager, with priority routing and a short DNS TTL.
compare.why: Front Door sits in the data path, so once probes mark an origin unhealthy, new requests go to the other region at once, whatever any resolver has cached. Traffic Manager with a short TTL narrows the gap and is a common design, but it only changes DNS answers: resolvers and browsers can hold cached answers past the TTL and probing intervals add delay, so a 30-second outcome cannot be assured.

compare.scenario: An order platform has a VM-based web tier and an Azure SQL database. If a region fails, the business needs service restored within one hour with at most five minutes of data loss, and does not want to pay for a second full production environment. Which is the better design?
compare.optionA: Run the full application in two regions behind Front Door, reworking the data tier to accept writes in both regions.
compare.optionB: Replicate the web VMs with Site Recovery and the database with an auto-failover group, starting compute on failover.
compare.why: Site Recovery and an auto-failover group deliver an RPO of seconds to minutes and recovery inside an hour, while the second region carries only replication and storage costs until a failover. Active-active would recover faster, but the targets do not need that speed, it roughly doubles running cost, and it would force a data-tier redesign to cope with concurrent writes.

compare.scenario: A retailer has 300 branch offices connecting by VPN, spread across eight regions, plus Azure workloads in each region. It needs any-to-any branch and VNet connectivity, with minimal manual routing work as sites are added. Which is the better design?
compare.optionA: Azure Virtual WAN, with a virtual hub in each region and branch VPN sites connected to the nearest hub.
compare.optionB: Hand-built hub-and-spoke, with VPN gateways in a hub VNet per region and the hubs peered together.
compare.why: Virtual WAN automates branch VPN onboarding at scale, hub-to-hub connectivity, and routing between sites and VNets, so each new branch or VNet connects without per-site route work. Hand-built hubs give full control and can cost less at small scale, but across 300 branches and eight regions every gateway, peering, and route table is manual effort that grows with each site.

compare.scenario: A team ships one containerized ASP.NET web API with steady daily traffic. They already run other apps on an App Service plan, want traffic shifted gradually during releases, and do not need scale-to-zero, event-driven scaling, or Dapr. Which is the better hosting choice?
compare.optionA: Azure Container Apps, with a new revision per release and traffic splitting for gradual releases.
compare.optionB: Azure App Service for Containers on the existing plan, using deployment slots for gradual releases.
compare.why: App Service on the existing plan reuses the team's tooling and plan capacity and covers gradual releases with deployment slots, so nothing more is needed. Container Apps would work and its revisions can split traffic too, but its strengths are scale-to-zero, event-driven scaling, and Dapr-based microservices, none of which are required, so the team would adopt a second platform for no benefit.

compare.scenario: When a file lands in a storage account, three independent systems must each react: one indexes it, one scans it, and one notifies a user. Each handles the blob-created event on its own, and no ordering is needed. Which is the better service?
compare.optionA: Azure Event Grid, with the storage account as the source and one event subscription per system.
compare.optionB: Azure Service Bus, with a topic that a publisher fills and one subscription per system.
compare.why: Blob-created events are published natively to Event Grid, which pushes each event to every subscriber with filtering and retry, with no polling and no publishing code. A Service Bus topic would also fan out reliably and is defensible, but something has to publish the messages, and its ordering, sessions, and transactions are capabilities this scenario does not use.
